💡 Key Takeaways

  • Nov 23, 2026 2 min read.
  • To address the challenge posed by modern iOS UI systems where the logical UI structure may not mirror the native UIKit hierarchy, LinkedIn engineers developed a view-agnostic analytics system build around a shared MeasurableNode contract.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News How LinkedIn Built a View-Agnostic Analytics System for Modern iOS UI Architectures.

Nov 23, 2026 2 min read.

To address the challenge posed by modern iOS UI systems where the logical UI structure may not mirror the native UIKit hierarchy, LinkedIn engineers developed a view-agnostic analytics system build around a shared MeasurableNode contract.

Sources indicate that as LinkedIn senior software engineer Keerthana Reddy Ragi explains, while traditional iOS analytics relies on UIView instances as the unit of measurement, modern UI architectures increasingly use flattened layouts and custom rendering systems where UI elements such as cards, sections, and containers are represented by virtual nodes that never materialize as UIViews. Consequently, analytics systems built solely around UIKit may fail to capture impressions for virtual nodes, lose logical hierarchy and contextual information, miscalculate visibility and impression duration, and attribute user actions to the wrong elements.

Recent findings suggest that linkedIn's solution introduces a shared MeasurableNode contract relaxing the requirement for every measurable element to be a UIView. A MeasurableNode exposes four properties: identity, geometry, hierarchy, and lifecycle.

As MeasurableNode is a shared contract, both traditional UIViews and virtual nodes can participate in the same analytics system. Indeed, while existing UIKit views continue using native UIKit properties and lifecycle hooks, virtual nodes explicitly provide the corresponding information to the same analytics layer.

The attach and detach methods are central to this approach, because they enable the layout or rendering system to notify the analytics system "when a node attaches, when its frame changes, and when it detaches". Unlike virtual nodes, UIKit already sends automatic lifecycle notifications to UIViews. Similarly, as virtual nodes are not directly recognized by UIKit as gesture-recognizer targets, the rendering framework must traverse the hybrid UIKit/virtual-node parent hierarchy to attribute user actions to the appropriate logical virtual node.

Ragi emphasizes that this design enables gradual adoption without requiring existing view-based analytics to be rewritten.

Teams can modernize one part of the UI without rewriting everything around it. Existing view-based analytics can keep working while newer virtual nodes use the latest contract.

LinkedIn engineers encountered three main challenges developing this approach to analytics. First, the widespread assumption that everything is a UIView is embedded in existing codebases. For example, "helper code that walked superviews, visibility checks that read frames directly from views, cleanup logic tied to view removal". All these cases had to be found and updated. Second, they had to strike the right balance between short-term compatibility and long-term correctness. Third, they needed to enforce the attach/detach discipline at the framework level.

Commenting on Ragi's article on LinkedIn, senior AI prompt engineer Artien Nadal observed:.

Industry observers note that I think there's a bigger opportunity here than just making analytics independent of the UI. What if teams could automatically detect when a UI change breaks event tracking or changes what an event actually means?

As a final note, although LinkedIn's implementation focused on UIKit, the underlying approach is far from being limited to it. With many apps now mixing UIKit and SwiftUI, cross-platform layout engines, or hybrid solutions, a view-agnostic analytics model based on a shared contract has broader applicability.

Industry News: How Supply Chain Leaders Can Separate Real AI Planning From the Hype

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (977 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gartner’s 2026 Hype Cycle for Agentic AI places AI agents at the Peak of Inflated Expectations.
  • Nearly every planning vendor now calls its product AI-powered, and many of the demos look alike: a chat window, a question about inventory, a quick answer.
  • In a recent development, take a common scenario: a shipment delay.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gartner’s 2026 Hype Cycle for Agentic AI places AI agents at the Peak of Inflated Expectations. Yet, the firm also predicted more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027, due to escalating costs, unclear business value or inadequate risk controls. Put together, those two findings describe a market where buyers are under pressure to adopt agents before they can tell which ones will hold up.

Nearly every planning vendor now calls its product AI-powered, and many of the demos look alike: a chat window, a question about inventory, a quick answer. A planner executive evaluating platforms has to work out which products will truly unlock fresh capability and which just put a flashy chatbot on top of a legacy SaaS.

In a recent development, take a common scenario: a shipment delay. In a traditional platform, a planner finds out about the delay via an exception report. They export data, upgrade formulas, rebuild the affected scenarios and present their recommendation in a cross-functional meeting. An AI assistant layered onto that process can proactively summarize the delay. The planner still has to rebuild the plan by hand to see what that suggestion does to other customers, material orders and warehouses.

Agents change the planning process by working from a shared, verifiable model of the business: supplier lead times, inventory targets, production constraints and allocation rules. When the delay comes in, an agent can immediately recalculate the plan, flags which SKUs and customers are now at risk, generates alternatives and highlights the downstream effect of each one. The planner’s work moves from assembling analysis to choosing between options. This enables a real transition from reactive to proactive planning.

This gap shows up fastest under pressure. Tesla faced a cash crunch with 400,000 pre-orders to deliver during the 2018 Model 3 production ramp, and planning had to change faster than the organization’s spreadsheets could keep up. The planning team built a 50-person planning engineering organization and its own software to connect sales and operations planning with day-to-day supply decisions, so a change in one part of the proposal flowed through everything it touched. Over the ramp, the team cut finished-goods inventory from 75 days to 15. Few companies can justify building a planning engineering team of that size. Well-built AI planning tools can give a lean planning team that same ability to replan the whole network when something shifts.

It has been revealed that A simple test for any vendor: when a planner asks why the system recommended a change, can it show the demand assumptions, incoming shipments and inventory calculations behind it? And can it show what else in the strategy moves if the planner accepts the recommendation?

Sources indicate that most of that hesitation comes down to a few practical problems. Planning data is scattered. Demand forecasts sit in one system, purchase orders in another, and supplier commitments often live in email threads and shared drives. An AI agent can only reason about the constraints it can see, so a tool connected to a partial picture will produce confident recommendations that miss the binding constraint.

According to recent reports, much of the most vital knowledge was never written down. Experienced planners know which suppliers run late in Q4, which customers get priority when inventory is tight, and which minimum order quantities can actually be negotiated. Until those rules are captured in the planning model, AI has nothing to work from but historical data.

According to recent reports, many teams also hand workflows to unsupervised agents too early. Edge cases that an experienced planner handles by instinct will break an agent that was never told about them. The projects that stick start with the planner who already does the work. That person defines the workflow, monitors the agent and approves what it produces at set checkpoints. Once planners build a daily habit with the tool, it stays in use, and the knowledge they’ve encoded becomes something the company owns.

It has been revealed that many planning teams will choose next year’s tools in the coming weeks, and vendor demos won’t make that choice easier. Planners are a skeptical lot by nature, and some vendor claims deserve extra skepticism.

According to recent reports, the clearest test is whether a tool can model your process, not the vendor’s. AI-native systems are composable by nature – they offer as much flexibility as a spreadsheet, with the power of an enterprise planning platform.

According to recent reports, here’s how to test it. Bring one workflow your team runs today, with its real quirks: how you allocate scarce inventory across customers, which suppliers get extra buffer, when a planner overrides the forecast. Ask the vendor to set it up on your data and walk through it. An AI-native platform can flex to fit how your team works and let you add steps as the process changes. If the answer is that your team will need to adapt to the system’s standard workflow, you are looking at a legacy platform with a chat window on top.

It has been revealed that michael Rossiter is co-founder and CEO of Atomic, an AI-native supply planning platform. He previously spent several years in Tesla’s supply chain organization, where he served as Director of Sales Operations and helped build the planning system that took Tesla through the Model 3 ramp. He is also a partner at DVx Ventures.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

Here's what changed, and what's next:.

The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:.

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:.

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:.

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code:.

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

In a recent development, reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them.

Sources indicate that API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

Sources indicate that while we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:.

Recent findings suggest that the first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:.

Industry observers note that and if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

Language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

John Harrington, Co-Founder & Chief Product Officer of HighByte – Interview Series

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that john Harrington is Co-Founder and Chief Product Officer of HighByte, where he leads business and product strategy, including product management and customer and partner success.
  • Industry observers note that highByte is an industrial software firm focused on the data architecture and integration challenges manufacturers face.
  • In a recent development, before co-founding HighByte in 2018, you held leadership roles at Kepware and PTC, and had worked alongside your fellow founders since 2012.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that john Harrington is Co-Founder and Chief Product Officer of HighByte, where he leads business and product strategy, including product management and customer and partner success. His career spans manufacturing operations and industrial software, giving him experience with both the challenges of using plant-floor data and the technology needed to connect it across an enterprise.

Industry observers note that highByte is an industrial software firm focused on the data architecture and integration challenges manufacturers face. Its Intelligence Hub provides an Industrial DataOps layer for connecting, modeling, contextualizing, and delivering operational data to enterprise applications, cloud platforms, and AI systems.

In a recent development, before co-founding HighByte in 2018, you held leadership roles at Kepware and PTC, and had worked alongside your fellow founders since 2012. What specific interoperability or security problem convinced you that manufacturers needed an entirely new industrial data platform, and how has that original vision evolved with the rise of AI?

It has been revealed that I’ve worked in manufacturing and industrial environments for nearly my entire career. In these roles, I’ve had the opportunity to view industrial data from both sides of the coin, working at a manufacturer that made data-driven decisions and a number of software providers that enable digitalization and smart manufacturing.

This is a significant challenge. For one thing, users often need data that is curated differently than how most execution systems—MES solutions, ERPs, data historians, or otherwise—choose to store it. If they are lucky, they might be able to copy data from these systems and paste it into Excel to be analyzed and compared. Unfortunately, this method takes a lot of time, delays their decision-making, and requires access to domain experts who can explain the nuances of the data being reviewed.

Luckily, today’s data storage and analysis systems are tremendous. Cloud platforms like AWS and Azure and data warehouse providers like Snowflake and Databricks have simplified the scale challenge, creating unified repositories for industrial data across plants and offering easy access for business customers through applications and LLMs. Still, there’s a larger need to link these capable operational systems with emerging cloud and AI solutions, which itself requires the automated delivery of usable, contextualized, and compliant data.

Like any other business, AI has had an impact on the way HighByte operates. On the one hand, we’ve incorporated AI into our platform, creating a Pipeline AI Agent and a Modeling Agent for LLM-assisted pipeline, model, and instance generation and management. But these solutions have also changed how customers use and interact with industrial data in their day-to-day operations. By establishing a foundation of connected, contextualized, high-quality data for our customers, we provide the critical information that LLMs and agents need to operate effectively and efficiently in manufacturing environments.

Industry observers note that manufacturers are often eager to deploy AI before addressing the condition of their underlying data. What does a robust Industrial DataOps strategy look like in practice, and what warning signs indicate that a company’s data foundation is not ready for AI?

It’s vital to note that any Industrial DataOps strategy should be part of an organization’s more comprehensive Industrial Data Strategy, which encompasses a broad view of organizational scope, applications, data platforms, integrations, networks, governance, and regulatory requirements. Within this larger strategy, a more targeted Industrial DataOps approach can address integration requirements and focus on delivering usable data to required applications based on established contracts and cadences. This involves creating a robust data foundation and defining standard data products and pipelines for each application or use case.

According to recent reports, any firm that lacks a strong data foundation will not be capable of successful AI deployment at scale. It’s as simple as that. An effective Industrial DataOps strategy is one that ensures data is contextualized, connected, governed, and trusted before it’s consumed by applications or AI models.

Manufacturers should be careful not to rush AI deployments if their data is not yet up to the task. The warning signs are easy to spot: siloed systems, inconsistent naming conventions, duplicate data pipelines, and teams spending more time and effort finding data than actually using it. If you’re still debating which version of your data is accurate, you’re not ready to implement and scale AI solutions.

Industry observers note that AI agents work best when they have very focused objectives and a limited number of capable tools at their disposal to access data. Overly broad agents with too many potential tools and unclear data resources will inevitably result in hallucinations and incorrect decisions, ultimately doing more harm than good.

Industrial data is frequently fragmented across programmable logic controllers, manufacturing execution systems, historians, enterprise applications, and cloud platforms. What context must be added to this raw data before an AI model or agent can reliably interpret it and make useful decisions?

Industry observers note that imagine if I dropped you in the middle of a supermarket and asked you to buy me the items that I need. No detail, no list, no direction. Even worse, the aisle markers and signage are nowhere to be found. What do you think the odds are that you’d get me exactly what I’m looking for?

In a recent development, this is the type of scenario that AI models and agents are likely to find themselves in without proper context. Even with access to raw manufacturing data, this information alone cannot provide sufficient guidance for AI models to take accurate and impactful action. They need as much context as possible in order to effectively carry out their assigned tasks and provide reliable output.

Going back to the supermarket example, imagine if I asked you to specifically buy the supplies I need to create a PB&J sandwich. You could walk into the store, find the proper aisles based on the clearly marked signage, and get me the bread, peanut butter, jelly, and a knife for spreading. Maybe even some potato chips on the side.

Sources indicate that in the same way, a predictive maintenance agent in an Industrial DataOps system can rely on clearly contextualized data to meet its needs. The agent can cite clearly marked temperature, pressure, and vibration data and compare it against historical performance, allowing it to recognize any relevant fluctuations and take preventative action as needed.

You have predicted that agentic AI could produce a hundredfold increase in edge-based data consumers, with specialized agents supporting maintenance, quality, scheduling, and supply chain operations. How must traditional factory data architecture change to support this scale without creating thousands of brittle integrations?

Recent findings suggest that traditional industrial data architectures were designed to support a handful of applications consuming data in each factory. Now, agentic AI is set to completely change that equation. Instead of managing dozens of data consumers, manufacturers will need to support thousands of automated, specialized agents moving forward.

It has been revealed that the answer here isn’t thousands of new point-to-point integrations. Instead, it’s a centralized data layer that can contextualize, govern, and securely deliver the right data product to the right consumer at the right time—regardless of whether it’s a human user or an automated agent. Accessibility, context, and governance will all be key for maximizing the full potential of AI solutions on the factory floor.

HighByte has introduced Model Context Protocol services that allow industrial data pipelines to be exposed as tools for AI agents. How does Model Context Protocol complement existing standards such as Open Platform Communications Unified Architecture, Message Queuing Telemetry Transport, and application programming interfaces, and what governance is required to prevent agents from accessing the wrong tools or data?

Sources indicate that OPC UA and MQTT were designed for reading and writing device-level data, while APIs were designed for interacting directly with applications. MCP was designed specifically for interacting with LLMs. The HighByte Intelligence Hub is a middleware layer that unites these protocols, interacting with each device, system, and agent using their preferred protocol and curating data products using data from one or more sources.

Just as importantly, Intelligence Hub creates a layer of control and governance between agents and operational systems. Rather than giving agents unrestricted access to data, manufacturers can govern what tools the agents can access, which systems they can interact with, and what kinds of decisions they can influence.

Traditionally, governance was applied in the application layer through user-role-based access controls. As manufacturers deploy more agents across maintenance, quality, scheduling, and supply chain operations, traditional applications go away and agent-specific governance becomes crucial. In an agentic ecosystem, the governance of data flows effectively becomes the mechanism for governing the overall actions of AI agents.

In a recent development, the Pipeline AI Agent in HighByte Intelligence Hub allows consumers to create, explain, and modify industrial data pipelines through natural language while retaining human review. Which DataOps responsibilities are well suited to AI automation, and where should human approval remain mandatory?

Deploying complex data pipelines is often iterative and, as a result, relatively challenging. With the HighByte Intelligence Hub, we have provided multiple modes for easily creating, modifying, and managing both modeling and pipeline configuration tasks. A user can manually create and modify their own configurations, leverage the Pipeline and Modeling Agents for AI-driven assistance, and use MCP configuration tools to fully configure the Intelligence Hub externally with an agent. We expect that the user will select the most appropriate method based on their experience level with the Intelligence Hub and AI and the size and scope of the changes.

According to recent reports, given all these methods of configuration, the system will need to be tested and validated. This is done in real time by agents that observe and approve any changes being applied. The agents are also great at explaining what the configuration does for troubleshooting and documentation purposes.

In a recent development, global manufacturers need common data standards across facilities, but every plant has different equipment, processes, and operational requirements. How can companies create reusable industrial data products while preserving the local context that makes the data meaningful?

It has been revealed that this is one of the core benefits of a robust Industrial DataOps strategy and platform. When different facilities are unified under a single platform, teams can align and standardize data collection and naming practices across different sites, while still maintaining the flexibility needed to account for site-specific context.

The key is to separate standardization from uniformity. Manufacturers should establish common enterprise models, naming conventions, and governance policies, but at the same time should still allow sites to capture the operational context unique to each facility’s processes and outputs. For example, a bottling line in one facility may operate differently than an equivalent line elsewhere, but both can still map to a shared enterprise data model.

HighByte recently partnered with Siemens to combine industrial edge connectivity, contextualized data, and tools for building AI models and agents. Does this type of collaboration signal that the future industrial AI stack will be built through interoperable ecosystems rather than a single end-to-end platform?

Yes, the future industrial AI stack won’t be owned by any one organization; it will be built on interoperable technologies that each solve a specific problem well. HighByte partnered with Siemens because we both recognized that successful industrial AI requires both operational connectivity and trusted, contextualized data. Together, Siemens Industrial Edge and HighByte Intelligence Hub help manufacturers bridge the gap between IT and OT systems; connecting data from machinery, SCADA, historians, MES, ERP and all the rest of the systems in and around the factory into a unified data infrastructure that AI can actually use.

AI agents are only as effective as the data they consume, and each operational system provides a piece of the puzzle for the agent, but not the entire puzzle. Open, interoperable ecosystems give manufacturers the flexibility to innovate with best-in-breed solutions without creating fresh silos or vendor lock-in. By combining Siemens’ industrial connectivity capacity with HighByte’s DataOps capabilities, manufacturers can more easily connect, contextualize, and consume industrial data to scale AI models and agents across the enterprise.

Predictive maintenance, quality inspection, energy optimization, and production planning are all frequently presented as promising industrial AI applications. How should manufacturers select their first use case, establish measurable business value, and avoid becoming trapped in a cycle of pilots that never scale?

It has been revealed that it’s essential that manufacturers start with a problem they need to solve, not a technology they want to adopt. The best first use case is one that is causing frustration today, has actual measurable business value, ties to accessible data, and has a clear path to operational adoption. Once that has been achieved, you can take your learnings and apply AI to tackle the next challenge.

Today, too many teams are focusing on deploying isolated pilots, when they should really be prioritizing the underlying data architecture that’s required to scale AI across systems, sites, and enterprise infrastructure. Success will come not from a single use case, but instead, from building a reusable foundation that supports multiple AI deployments over time and expands in tandem with increasing AI integration.

Looking ahead, how do you expect AI agents to change the roles of plant operators, engineers, and data teams, and what technical or organizational barrier must be solved before manufacturers can safely give these systems greater autonomy?

I don’t foresee a world where AI agents fully replace manufacturing professionals, but I do see one where AI changes how they work. With the support of effective agents, operators will be able to spend less time searching for information and more time making impactful, informed decisions. Engineers will be tasked with overseeing and optimizing fleets of highly specialized agents, and data teams will shift from report building to data product and AI system governance.

The real differentiator in this AI-driven future will be how effectively manufacturers can deploy and govern specialized agents that can take autonomous action on trusted industrial data for real business challenges. Those who solve the data and governance challenge early will be the ones who realize the greatest value from AI. The ultimate value of AI for manufacturers is to reduce downtime, increase throughput, reduce defects and scrap, improve safety, reduce costs, and improve the agility of the business to react to supply and demand changes.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, if you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX.
  • According to recent reports, TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit.
  • TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, if you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

According to recent reports, TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch users had to work harder to get in.

Industry observers note that until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

In a recent development, to make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

TorchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:.

Industry observers note that the extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

Recent findings suggest that transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

In a recent development, the model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

In a recent development, TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

Industry observers note that models too significant for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:.

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1.

The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

Sources indicate that TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:.

It has been revealed that the bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

In a recent development, decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

We're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

It has been revealed that the Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

In a recent development, it's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an problem on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 concerns, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel aims. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch consumers. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

Sources indicate that we can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an problem and tell us about it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TIDAL will begin removing all wholly AI-generated tracks from its catalog on December 9, 2026, Robert Andersen revealed on November 24, 2026. He mentioned the initiative would delete 29 million songs and leave the catalog clear of those tracks by the beginning of 2027.

Andersen’s X profile indicates he runs TIDAL at Block, while Block’s leadership page identifies him as the company’s principal designer. TIDAL’s official account confirmed the start date on X, writing, “Bye AI music. Starting December 9.”.

Andersen remarked TIDAL tagged and demonetized all wholly AI-generated tracks a few months earlier to protect real artists’ authenticity, but that 43% of tracks distributed to the service in the preceding 90 days had been detected as AI-generated and 96% of AI-generated songs received zero plays. Those figures describe a large detected inflow with little listening for AI-generated material. The latest policy adds deletion to the earlier labeling and demonetization approach.

It has been revealed that andersen estimated that TIDAL would reject 80,000 to 85,000 AI-generated songs per day, described the organization as the first digital service provider to take this step, and encouraged competing services to follow. The daily figure covers expected future rejections, distinct from deletions of music already in the catalog.

TIDAL’s terms, effective June 29, 2026, for the service outside Canada, the European Union, the European Economic Area and the United Kingdom, define AI-generated content as audio wholly or substantially generated by generative AI with limited or no direct human creative input beyond an initial text prompt or similar instruction. The unveiled removal applies to wholly AI-generated tracks, a narrower formulation than that contractual definition.

It has been revealed that those terms provide for an in-app AI indicator at track or album level. Identification and labeling are performed on a best-efforts basis using industry-standard detection technology; TIDAL cautions that detection can produce false positives and false negatives and does not warrant the accuracy or completeness of a label or its absence.

Under the same terms, TIDAL Upload tracks may be scanned for AI generation, AI-generated uploads are ineligible for monetization, and users who believe a track was erroneously tagged can contact support. The rules already give classification direct financial consequences for uploaders.

TIDAL’s published content guidelines say the service accepts AI-generated content that meets additional requirements. For AI-generated content, they prohibit material that impersonates or imitates an artist’s voice, likeness or identity without express authorization, misleads listeners about its origin or creation, or perpetuates streaming fraud, including inflated play counts and royalties diverted from legitimate artists.

Industry observers note that violations may be labeled, demonetized or removed without prior notice, while repeated or egregious breaches can bring account suspension or termination. Moderation combines automated scanning at upload with human review when necessary. Consumers can appeal content removals and account decisions, with human moderators reassessing the material and initial decision; account suspensions and terminations also receive human review before being finalized.

The announcement moves TIDAL beyond disclosure and demonetization toward using AI detection to determine catalog access. Since the published terms acknowledge mistaken classifications, the policy’s practical impact will depend on how reliably TIDAL distinguishes wholly generated music from human-directed work and how effectively its review process handles disputes.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1273 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow.
  • This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience.
  • Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:.

Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

The Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda. The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating New Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:.

Sources indicate that the modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

It has been revealed that neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

In a recent development, after profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

You profile three implementations of the same operation:.

The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory.

Start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:.

The schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

Call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.

After profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.

The key averages table highlights that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

The table shows which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.

Each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x * x, x * rms, and the final multiplication by weight. aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root.

Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

Sources indicate that in Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running.

The system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:.

In eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

Replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:.

The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

Recent findings suggest that in the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile.

With @torch.compile(backend="neuron"), TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.

The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

According to recent reports, the table reveals one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

Both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.

Sources indicate that key_averages() highlights which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost.

In a recent development, in Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

Tech Report: QCon San Francisco 2026: Securing AI Agents in Production

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (681 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: Securing AI Agents in Production.
  • Nov 23, 2026 3 min read.
  • Industry observers note that securing AI agents is a variation of the insider-risk problem, requiring distinct identities, narrowly scoped credentials and fine-grained policy controls, according to Amanda Walker, senior director of engineering for privacy, safety and security at Google.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: Securing AI Agents in Production.

Nov 23, 2026 3 min read.

Industry observers note that securing AI agents is a variation of the insider-risk problem, requiring distinct identities, narrowly scoped credentials and fine-grained policy controls, according to Amanda Walker, senior director of engineering for privacy, safety and security at Google. In a QCon San Francisco session, she outlined patterns for teams whose agents have been adopted organically and are running ahead of their security and observability frameworks.

With agents now executing multi-step plans in live production environments, Walker argued that "a rogue AI agent is the same problem as a rogue human insider," one that acts with superhuman speed and persistence. Controls therefore need to work at machine speed, rather than relying on someone reviewing logs the next morning. She covered identity and credentials, boundary defence, subagent orchestration and policy-based containment.

Walker described giving an agent raw human credentials as the fastest path to production failure. The agent inherits the user's authority, so a prompt injection in a document can turn that access to an attacker's purposes. She recommended explicit principals for agents, the AI equivalent of service accounts, so each agent can be provisioned and logged separately without impersonating anyone.

Scoped OAuth tokens limit an agent's access in time and scope, but are immutable once issued. With credential attenuation, an orchestrator instead mints narrower tokens for its subagents, such as read-only access to logs, or read-only access to a repository between two commits when bisecting a broken build.

She pointed to Eclipse Biscuit, a token format whose holders can append restrictions, but cannot remove existing ones without invalidating its signature. It takes more work than reusing human authentication infrastructure, but suits services where teams control both ends.

For API keys, a proxy can give the agent a short-lived synthetic key and substitute the real one as traffic leaves, protecting it from prompt injection and exfiltration.

Walker cautioned that a virtual machine protects the host, not the resources an agent can reach: an agent with network access can still delete a database. Container sandboxes, ephemeral runtimes and sidecar proxies such as Envoy give finer control over file system and network access. But "a perfectly isolated compute sandbox is not useful," she said, so teams need policies that constrain what agents do with the services they call.

She also highlighted poisoned skills on public marketplaces that steal API keys and cryptocurrency wallets, citing Snyk research that found more than a third of publicly available skills had at least one security flaw.

Agents also cause harm by being wrong rather than malicious. Walker described an agent that read internal SRE documentation and invoked a break-glass process intended for emergencies, having decided it was the most expedient route. Monitoring caught it, but the lesson was that organisations must distinguish agents from the people they work for, because some processes depend on a human accepting risk. For the same reason, she described computer-use agents, which drive a mouse and keyboard, as in essence impersonation, while acknowledging they solve problems that machine protocols such as MCP cannot.

Asked in the question-and-answer session about tagging identities as agents, Walker said: "The biggest thing it gave us was auditability about some of these risk decisions." The distinction supports human-only rules, such as emergency access, and can help with agent-only rules, such as signed releases in regulated environments, although she noted that an agent flag alone is not enough for those.

In the Q&A, she also advised security teams not to simply say no, which pushes colleagues to work around controls, but to allow experimentation where mistakes are reversible and keep human review for irreversible actions such as wire transfers.

How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2216 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.
  • In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens.
  • The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.

In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model.

The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step.

Industry observers note that one of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency.

In a recent development, the model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses.

Recent findings suggest that we rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication.

Industry observers note that the leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense.

For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once.

According to recent reports, the first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request.

Sources indicate that the second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses.

Sources indicate that the natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill.

Industry observers note that to see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill, the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode, the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth.

This effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading.

Industry observers note that think of a shipping organization that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings.

The third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model.

And the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows.

According to recent reports, adapting a model's vocabulary is not a latest idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations.

Recent findings suggest that they choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve.

They work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one.

VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first.

First, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly.

Second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping tech giant: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget.

To find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points.

Recent findings suggest that third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain.

In a recent development, an expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents reveals up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated.

In a recent development, A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running.

That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%.

To measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime.

According to recent reports, the model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810.

Getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version.

In a recent development, the lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter.

It has been revealed that to find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling.

VocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803.

It has been revealed that vocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe.

Specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary.

The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon.
