    #183791. Breaking: 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1858 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1858 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation.
    • According to recent reports, I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally.
    • Sources indicate that orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation.

    According to recent reports, I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory.

    Sources indicate that orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk.

    I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me.

    My first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through pi. That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim.

    When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.

    Recent findings suggest that strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090!

    It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp, at 13.5 tok/s.

    That's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed.

    It has been revealed that before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token?

    Sources indicate that llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the CPU (--cpu-moe, --n-cpu-moe N, -ot "exps=CPU", or --fit on to pick for you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache (--moe-cache-mib) just landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses ~10% even when everything fits.

    vLLM's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels read them in place over PCIe. For a MoE layer, that's only the routed experts, but nothing is cached: a hot expert crosses PCIe again on every token, and there's no disk tier. By default the offloaded weights include dense layers, read on every token; --cpu-offload-params experts keeps it to the experts. That fits vLLM's substantial batches, which touch almost every expert anyway, less so one user on one GPU.

    It has been revealed that transformers offloads through Accelerate (device_map="auto", offload_folder), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU before forward. For a MoE, that module is a layer's whole expert bank, so every token copies every expert of every offloaded layer to use 8 or 10 of them. No cache, no notion of routing. And on a Mac, CPU and GPU share the same memory, so "offload to CPU" frees nothing.

    I ran all of them on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB), with plenty of RAM, and Harry Mellor reran vLLM with better flags:.

    Industry observers note that offloading only the experts doubles vLLM's speed, and FP8 helps on top (half the bytes per expert, more of the model on the GPU). vLLM's other offload backend, which copies groups of layers ahead of time, ran under 1 tok/s.

    Sources indicate that if the experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat. If they don't, you have to stream only what the router picks, through a bounded cache, fast enough that the SSD is the bottleneck and not Python, ideally reusing the model's fast expert kernels. That's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac, and Transformers couldn't do it out of the box.

    In a recent development, strata was already too slow for me on the laptop, and Transformers was not going to beat it anytime soon. But the Accelerate path was so far off that I wanted to try fixing offloading in Transformers itself, with the massive model on my laptop as the target, knowing it would probably stay too slow for how I work.

    All of the code was built with AI: the Transformers PR, the model-specific package and the Metal kernels. My part was choosing what to try, reading the profiles, and deciding what to keep. Everything is in a Space: tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming.

    I started with OLMoE-1B-7B, which fits in memory, so I could compare every token with vanilla Transformers.

    According to recent reports, first version: experts on disk, an LRU cache on the device, and a Python loop running one expert at a time. With every expert already cached, it did 10.1 tok/s. Vanilla did ~32. The I/O was fine, my loop was not: vanilla uses grouped_mm, which runs all the experts of a layer in one kernel.

    Sources indicate that the fix, and the key idea of this project, was to turn the cache into a slot pool: one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers, plus a per-layer table from expert id to slot. Remap the router's expert ids to slots and the pool looks like a regular expert bank, so grouped_mm runs on it as is. No custom expert matmul needed. That got it to 34.6 tok/s, against 38.1 for vanilla.

    Industry observers note that I then turned the standalone loader into an option of from_pretrained, in huggingface/transformers#50717. To try it, install Transformers from that PR:.

    Then, moving from OLMoE to the real target, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next:.

    That repo holds the output of the project's conversion script: the dense weights, the experts quantized to 3 bits, and the n-gram table.

    Industry observers note that experts mapped to "disk" go through the streaming path instead of Accelerate's offload: the loader skips their tensors and MoE layers switch to an offloaded implementation. Misses are read by 8 I/O threads, one contiguous read per expert. The next two layers' routers run early on the current hidden states to guess which experts to prefetch. Experts can be quantized offline so reads are smaller. It works for MoE models with the standard experts layout.

    The API is still being discussed with the Transformers maintainers. The device_map form came out of that, and quantized experts will probably go through the per-layer quantization proposal of #50245 rather than their own option.

    Sources indicate that qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 48 layers of 512 experts (10 active), 121 GB in FP8. Streaming them isn't enough: there's also a 51 GB n-gram embedding table that needs its own disk path. So:.

    In a recent development, the conversion takes ~5 hours. After loading, it uses ~18 GiB, and a 6K prompt peaks at 25.4 GiB. That's about the limit: I have to close the browser, or macOS starts swapping.

    According to recent reports, the model-specific bits (the n-gram table, Metal kernels) live in a small package, moe-expert-streaming, on top of the PR. The first version ran at about 10 tok/s.

    Then I installed Strata on the same M5, with the same prompts:.

    Strata 0.1.60 used IQ3_XXS experts. Both ran greedy, with thinking, MTP and speculative drafts off, and 1,024-token prefill chunks. The full setup and raw results are on the Space's details page.

    I also tried vllm-metal, vLLM on Apple GPUs through MLX, which recently got expert offloading. It streams the routed experts from an MLX checkpoint through a bounded cache, like this project. But it can't run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on 32 GB, for the n-gram reason above: only the experts are streamed, and the n-gram tables stay in memory. That's 32 GB in the MLX checkpoints on the Hub, before the ~5 GB of dense layers and any expert cache.

    Most of the time wasn't spent on experts. Here's what helped:.

    Here's one MoE layer for one token, as it runs now:.

    These are the final results after these optimizations on the same M5 with the same prompts:.

    That's about 6% behind Strata on short decode, with slightly faster prefill, all through Transformers.

    Most of what's left is host round trips, ~10 ms per token. Waking up after a sync is only ~1 ms of that. The rest is the GPU running dry while Python queues the next layer. Strata queues the whole token's work up front, and the GPU waits on a Metal shared event at each layer while the host reads experts. PyTorch doesn't expose that. I tried to fake it with a kernel spinning on a flag the CPU writes, and the GPU took anywhere from a second to never to see the write. The real fix would be a native op on PyTorch's MPS stream, with a risk of hangs, so I haven't built it.

    Recent findings suggest that it runs at ~14 tok/s, close to Strata, and it's still too slow for how I use coding agents. Orthrus keeps doing the real work.

    Recent findings suggest that transformers didn't beat Strata, and closing the last ~6% would take deeper changes in the stack, starting with control over that per-layer sync, which PyTorch doesn't give you today. The interesting part is how it got that close: streaming only the routed experts, a bounded cache that grouped_mm runs on as is, and a few targeted Metal kernels. There's no C++ extension in the project: just Python, Metal kernels compiled at runtime with torch.mps.compile_shader, and prebuilt kernels from the Hub. All the Metal kernels written for this experiment are now published on the Hub, and the project loads them from there.

    Recent findings suggest that beating Strata was never the only goal, though. Building this was a great way to learn how MoEs and LLMs work from a systems perspective: how sparse the routing really is, how much an expert cache buys you, where memory bandwidth goes per token, and how much time the host and the GPU spend waiting on each other. Transformers makes all of that easy to poke at, one module at a time.

    Industry observers note that the generic expert streaming implementation is in huggingface/transformers#50717, and the benchmarks are in the Space. Feedback on the approach and the API is welcome.

    Thanks to Pedro, Lysandre and Arthur for their excellent feedback, and to Harry for helping test vLLM.

    Finally, thanks to Niko Veit for Strata. Strata set the bar for what's possible with expert streaming on consumer hardware, and having those numbers to chase is what pushed this work as far as it went.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry.
    • It has been revealed that if you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts.
    • In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

    It has been revealed that if you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

    In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

    SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

    The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension.

    In a recent development, ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The firm was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

    Direct Comparisons: Ahrefs vs SEMrush.

    Sources indicate that now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

    Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need promptly.

    In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

    Time-Series Models in the Streamhouse: A New Frontier and Use Cases

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2071 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads.
    • In a recent development, every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory.
    • The challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads. Now available natively on Confluent, in the cloud and on premises, running on CPUs.

    In a recent development, every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory. These observations form time series, and they carry signals that can help teams anticipate what happens next.

    The challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter. A forecast delivered after a production run, a stockout, or a payment authorization may be accurate, but too late to influence the outcome.

    IBM and Confluent are bringing time-series foundation models closer to the data as it flows. With Apache Flink, teams can apply forecasting , anomaly detection and semantic intelligence to streaming data using SQL, making model outputs available to the applications and people responsible for the next action.

    Foundation models have changed how organizations work with text, images, and documents. Time-series foundation models extend a similar idea to numerical data by learning general patterns from diverse historical data and then applying that knowledge to new series and tasks. The models can provide a starting point without requiring teams to train a separate model for every series. Depending on the task and deployment, teams can also fine-tune a model or combine its outputs with other data and business logic.

    Figure 1. More than 50 million downloads, and the family of four models behind them.

    Now the time series foundation models run natively inside Confluent as built-in functions in the cloud and on premises. In Confluent Cloud they are fully managed, with nothing to deploy (documentation). On premises, the models can run within your own infrastructure using Confluent Platform for Apache Flink.(documentation). The models run on CPUs, without requiring GPUs.

    The models can support a range of mission-critical use cases, from helping keep production lines in spec and detecting unusual store activity to improving product-level planning. They can also provide signals to assess card payments and forecast trading volume to help place large orders. These building blocks can be applied across manufacturing, retail, banking, and airlines, bringing insights closer to where decisions are made.

    See how time series and real-time context come together to create value:.

    Sources indicate that businesses operate continuously. Orders are updated, payments arrive, shipments are delayed, and inventory changes throughout the day. Yet the information behind these events often sits across systems that enhancement at different times or rely on periodic batch processes. When applications and AI agents act on outdated or inconsistent information, they risk making decisions that no longer reflect what is happening.

    In a recent development, A Streamhouse addresses this by continuously capturing, processing, governing, and serving current business context. Confluent’s Data Streaming Platform brings together five capabilities—connect, stream, process, govern, and query—to make that context available to applications, analytics, and agents. Apache Flink transforms and enriches data as it flows, while Lightning Tables provide low-latency access to the current state.

    Figure 2. The Streamhouse on Confluent: from existing data sources to current business context that agents, applications, analytics and lakehouses use anywhere.

    Sources indicate that time-series models add predictive power to this architecture. Flink can prepare the data, invoke forecasting and anomaly detection, and make the results available alongside the events that produced them. Other models—including large language models, statistical models, and specialized machine learning systems—can contribute where appropriate.

    According to recent reports, figure 3. The intelligence layer of the Streamhouse: time series models, large language models, and ML and statistical models, with orchestration across them.

    This approach can help teams in four ways:.

    It has been revealed that -Scale model development. A pretrained model can provide a common starting point across many time series, reducing the need to develop and maintain a separate model for each one.

    -Refresh predictions as data changes. Forecasts can incorporate recent observations as part of a streaming workflow, subject to the model’s requirements and the pipeline’s configuration.

    Sources indicate that -Put signals closer to decisions. Forecasts and anomalies can be routed to operational applications sooner, where teams can combine them with business context, rules, and human judgment.

    Industry observers note that -Run compact models on CPUs. The models are small enough to run on standard CPUs alongside the streaming pipeline, in the cloud or on premises, which can reduce the need for dedicated GPU infrastructure and simplify deployment.

    Recent findings suggest that figure 4. Stream native time-series intelligence on Confluent.

    The following scenarios illustrate how organizations could combine time-series models, streaming data, and application logic.

    According to recent reports, an ice cream line’s quality depends on overrun—the amount of air whipped into the mix. Today, the process engineer and operator rely on QA lab measurements taken after the tubs are filled. If a new cream lot or a warm, humid day changes the process, hours of production may already need rework by the time the team sees the result.

    To get ahead of the problem, a pretrained TTM model reads SCADA telemetry and QA measurements every 10 minutes. It forecasts the share of tubs expected to be in spec four hours ahead, along with a likely range.

    When the forecast falls below the plant’s target, an optimization process evaluates combinations of freezer draw temperature and airflow. Because the model takes these control variables as inputs, it can score each option before anything changes on the line. The operator approves the recommended setpoints, while routine adjustments can be automated within predefined guardrails.

    It has been revealed that the outcome is a more proactive process: less rework, lower energy use per tonne, and more consistent quality. The same approach can be applied to ovens, dryers, kilns, and mills.

    Sources indicate that figure 5. A forecast of product quality helps the operator evaluate freezer setpoints before making an adjustment.

    Recent findings suggest that A store operations team monitors sales for thousands of products across hundreds of stores. Fixed thresholds often flag predictable weekend peaks while missing quieter changes, such as a product selling less than expected. As alerts accumulate, it becomes harder for the team to know where to focus.

    In a recent development, AI_DETECT_ANOMALIES gives each sales series an expected range based on its recent history. Each upcoming reading is compared with that range at a confidence level the team chooses, without training a separate model for every product and store.

    When sales fall outside the expected range, the signal can be combined with inventory and store data to help identify a likely cause and recommend a next step—for example, checking the shelf or replenishing stock. The same approach can be applied to machine sensors, API telemetry, meter readings, and payment volumes.

    Figure 6. Store sales are compared with an expected range. In the view shown, recurring peaks remain within the range and no anomaly is flagged.

    According to recent reports, A category planner and a replenishment team need to keep products available across every store without carrying excess inventory. But forecasts may be refreshed only once a week, often focusing on top-selling products, while the long tail is managed with simpler rules. When sales patterns change between planning cycles, one store can run out while another has too much stock.

    With AI_FORECAST, a pretrained model can forecast demand across products and stores. In this example, it produces a 28-day forecast with a P10–P90 range, refreshed as new sales data arrives. The planning application combines the forecast with inventory, lead time, and the planner’s chosen service level to calculate a reorder point.

    Industry observers note that when stock is projected to fall below that point, an agent can draft a purchase order for review. The same approach can support planning for spare parts, staffing, ATM cash, and energy demand.

    Recent findings suggest that figure 7. A store-level demand forecast informs a reorder point and a proposed purchase order for oat milk.

    Fraud teams already rely on sophisticated rules and models to evaluate transactions. One continuing challenge is that a threshold applied across many cardholders may not reflect how each person normally spends.

    Sources indicate that A time-series signal can add that individual context. In this example, each payment is compared with an expected spending range based on the card’s recent history. A transaction outside that range is passed to the bank’s existing fraud systems as an additional input, alongside other signals and business rules.

    The bank can then decide whether to approve the payment, request additional authentication, or investigate further. The decision and the signals behind it can be retained for review.

    Figure 8.A payment outside the card’s expected spending range prompts a step-up authentication in an illustrative fraud workflow.

    An execution desk needs to divide a large order into smaller trades while managing its effect on the market. Historical volume curves offer a starting point, but today’s trading activity may look very different from the average.

    In a recent development, on each one-minute bar, PatchTST-FM forecasts trading volume for the next 30 minutes, with a P10–P90 range. The execution algorithm uses that forecast to pace the order within the participation limit set by the desk.

    If a news event changes market activity, the algorithm can pause and replan. If trading is quieter than expected, it can reduce the size of each slice and signal that the order may take longer to complete. Each forecast and the resulting execution decisions can be retained in the audit trail.

    Figure 9. Volume forecast informs the proposed execution schedule for a 100,000-share order.

    A reliability engineer investigating an unusual sensor pattern may want to know whether similar behavior appeared elsewhere in the plant.

    Sources indicate that TSPulse can produce representations of time-series windows that support similarity search. In a separately built application, those representations could be indexed and used to retrieve historical patterns across equipment. An engineer could search for shapes such as a spike and recovery, a gradual rise, or a step change, then inspect the associated maintenance records and operating conditions.

    This application requires an embedding pipeline, an index, and access to the relevant context. Similarity can help narrow an investigation; it does not establish a root cause by itself.

    Figure 10. Time-series embeddings can support a search for similar patterns across equipment and other signals.

    The same models and building blocks can support different workflows across industries:.

    In a recent development, figure 11. The plant twin, from sensor to setpoint. A latest cream lot pulls overrun off target. The forecast reads the line, the agent proposes a new draw temperature and air flow, the operator approves, and the tubs are back in spec. Simulated data.

    Figure 12. The store twin, a store and its supply chain. A promo is coming for oat milk. The forecast prices in the promo and sets the reorder point, the agent raises a purchase order, the planner approves, and the shelf is full on promo day. Simulated data.

    Banking: payments and the trading desk. The fraud lead wants to stop card testing without blocking good customers, and the trader wants a large order done without moving the price. Every card and every symbol is scored against its own expected pattern, event by event. Fraud and security holds the odd swipe before authorization, anomaly detection spots the unusual flow, and trading paces each order with the forecast volume.

    Airlines: hub operations, fleet and network. Operations control wants to see a disruption coming while there is still time to act. Engine, gate and network streams are forecast and checked in real time. Anomaly detection catches the engine reading that drifts, production optimization rebalances gates and crews, and supply chain planning puts the spare part where the aircraft will be.

    In every industry, the Streamhouse does the same work: Flink runs the Granite models to forecast, detect and optimize, Streaming Agents act on the live context, and people approve the exceptions.

    Explore the models on Confluent to see how time-series intelligence can support real-time decisions.

    Code and notebooks: github.com/ibm-granite/granite-tsfm.

    #183787. Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1390 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1390 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.
    • A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models.
    • GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.

    A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models. The full version will be on arXiv soon.

    GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today. Anyone running a shared cluster has to decide, every day, which jobs go on which GPUs and in what order. That plan is only as good as the estimate of how long each job will take. When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips, experiments wait and delivery dates move.

    Sources indicate that better duration estimates turn this into planning instead of guesswork: what runs, when, and on how many GPUs, with less idle capacity in between. Yet the estimate most teams use is a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation. It says nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon.

    We wanted to know how far off that math really is, and whether we could do better before a job is even dispatched. So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors.

    The short version: the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do. The regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs.

    In a recent development, for a dense Transformer, training costs roughly 6·P·D floating-point operations, where P is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. Divide that by what your GPUs can deliver and you get a training-loop time:.

    Industry observers note that here N_GPU is the number of GPUs, FLOPS_peak is the peak throughput of one GPU from its spec sheet, and MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is the fraction of that peak the training actually achieves. Real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance.

    This is a good description of the optimization loop. A job is more than its loop, though. Before the first step there is environment setup, model download and loading, and tokenization. During training there are periodic evaluations and checkpoint uploads. At the end, the final model goes to object storage. On a multi-tenant cluster, all of it competes with other jobs for network and storage I/O.

    These overheads depend on configuration, and they do not scale neatly with workload or GPU count. Two jobs with the same nominal compute can finish hours apart.

    To keep the comparison fair, the FLOP baseline we test counts the scheduled evaluation tokens as well as the training tokens, and we sweep MFU over a wide range.

    We treat end-to-end duration as a supervised regression problem. Given a feature vector built from the job configuration and model metadata, predict the wall-clock time between the moment the job gets its GPUs and the moment it is done. Queue time is excluded.

    Two design choices shaped the work:.

    We compared Linear Regression, Ridge, XGBoost and CatBoost. Feature selection combined correlation filtering, mutual information and permutation importance across 18 candidate feature sets, followed by a grid search with MAE as the criterion. The final CatBoost model uses 24 features.

    It has been revealed that distribution of end-to-end duration across the 272 runs. Mean 23.43 h, median 15.29 h.

    All numbers come from stratified 5-fold cross-validation. The first four rows are analytical and involve no fitting.

    Recent findings suggest that no single MFU value fixes the FLOP baseline. We swept MFU from 0.25 to 0.65. The best setting, 30%, still leaves a mean error above 12 hours on jobs that last 23 hours on average.

    A more detailed analytical model does not close the gap. As a second baseline we took Calculon (Isaev et al., SC '23), an analytical performance model for LLM training from prior work. It builds an explicit layer graph and accounts for compute, memory traffic and inter-device communication. We extended the public implementation to cover LoRA, grouped-query attention, fused attention, bfloat16 and SwiGLU. Its estimates still correspond to a median of only 11% of the observed wall-clock time. That claims nothing against Calculon as a step-level tool, which is what it was designed for. It shows how much of a production job happens outside the optimization step.

    In a recent development, linear models help, and then stall. Ridge brings MAE down to 7.23 h. The relationship between configuration and duration is not well captured by a purely linear model.

    According to recent reports, gradient boosting does the heavy lifting. CatBoost and XGBoost land within one standard deviation of each other on every metric. We carry CatBoost forward because it has the lowest mean error across the board.

    In a recent development, catBoost's feature importance concentrates in a handful of features. Model and workload variables are there, as expected, but so are evaluation and checkpoint variables. num_eval_data, the total number of samples processed in evaluation over the life of the job, ranks first, followed by num_trainable_params, batch_eval_size_percent, num_all_params and num_gpus*batch_train_percent, with num_params_saved close behind. SHAP values tell the same story: high evaluation volume consistently pushes the predicted time up, while trainable parameter count has a nonlinear effect that only becomes large for the biggest models.

    Mean feature importance of the CatBoost model across folds (PredictionValuesChange).

    Recent findings suggest that feature importance is not a causal claim. Still, the pattern lines up with how a job is actually spent. How often you evaluate, how large the evaluation set is and how many checkpoints you persist all shape the wall-clock time, alongside model and dataset scale. These are choices people often make by habit when writing a training config.

    Sources indicate that one caveat on reading the plots: larger GPU allocations show positive contributions to predicted time. In our data, bigger allocations go with bigger jobs, so num_gpus acts partly as a proxy for job scale. It does not mean adding GPUs makes a job slower.

    Sources indicate that looking at all 272 out-of-fold predictions, the median absolute error is 0.51 h. 80% of predictions are within 2.20 h and 90% are within 4.31 h. Broken down by job duration:.

    Up to 60 hours, the median error stays at about one hour or less. The long tail is where the model struggles, and with only 13 runs above 60 hours we read that as a data limitation.

    Out-of-fold absolute error against real duration, colored by duration range. Errors stay low up to 60 h and widen in the sparse tail.

    According to recent reports, more data should still help. On a fixed 20% holdout, MAE drops from 1.63 h to 1.50 h when going from 85% to 100% of the training partition, with no clear plateau.

    In practice, the predictor gives a scheduler a duration it can strategy around before a job starts: which jobs to run together, when GPUs will free up, and whether a run will finish in time for its deadline.

    What does transfer is the method: overhead-aware features, multicollinearity-aware selection and the comparison protocol. The full paper will report the feature formulas, the selection procedure, the search spaces and the final hyperparameters in full, so the pipeline can be rebuilt on any execution-log dataset with a similar structure.

    Next on our list: hardware-specific descriptors and validation on other GPU types, transfer learning for configurations with few observations, other training objectives, and more data on long runs.

    Sources indicate that the full paper is coming to arXiv soon. Follow the Dharma-AI organization on Hugging Face to be notified when it is out, and leave your questions in the comments below. We would like to hear how you estimate job duration on your own clusters.

    Dharma-AI R&D · We Make AI Your Model.

    #183786. Why Your FastAPI + SQLAlchemy App Chokes Under Load (And How to Fix N+1 & Pool Exhaustion)

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (384 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    Why Your FastAPI + SQLAlchemy App Chokes Under Load (And How to Fix N+1 & Pool Exhaustion)

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (384 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that your FastAPI service runs effortlessly in local development with 50ms response times.
    • In nine out of ten Python backends, this is not a hardware limit—it is a combination of lazy-loaded N+1 queries and holding database sessions open across slow I/O.
    • Here is how to diagnose and fix both bottlenecks cleanly.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that your FastAPI service runs effortlessly in local development with 50ms response times. Then you deploy it to production, hit 150 concurrent requests, and suddenly latency spikes to 8 seconds before throwing QueuePool limit of size 5 overflow 10 reached, connection timed out.

    In nine out of ten Python backends, this is not a hardware limit—it is a combination of lazy-loaded N+1 queries and holding database sessions open across slow I/O.

    Here is how to diagnose and fix both bottlenecks cleanly.

    By default, ORMs like SQLAlchemy load relationships lazily. When you serialize a list of 100 orders and access order.customer.email inside a loop or Pydantic response model, Python executes 101 separate SQL queries instead of one.

    The Fix: Use selectinload() (for one-to-many collections) or joinedload() (for many-to-one foreign keys) to fetch related records in a single round-trip:.

    In async SQLAlchemy (AsyncSession), explicitly setting lazy="raise" on model relationships is a great guardrail—it forces an immediate error in development whenever code accidentally triggers an implicit query.

    Database connections are expensive, finite resources. A classic mistake in FastAPI endpoints is injecting db: AsyncSession = Depends(get_db) at the top of a route, fetching a record, and then calling an external payment or AI API while the transaction is still open:.

    The Fix: Split the database work into two short-lived sessions—read first, release the connection back to the pool, perform the slow HTTP call, and open a fresh session only for the final write.

    Managed databases (RDS, Neon, Supabase) silently drop idle TCP connections behind load balancers. Without health checks, your workers grab dead sockets and crash with InterfaceError or OperationalError.

    Configure your async engine with explicit pool bounds and pre-ping validation:.

    Industry observers note that updating 5,000 rows inside a Python for loop generates 5,000 individual UPGRADE statements and massive transaction log overhead. Use SQLAlchemy Core update() statements or insert().values(batch) so Postgres executes the mutation in a single query plan.

    Enable SQL echo logging locally (echo=True) or assert query counts in your pytest suite—if a single list endpoint fires more than 2–3 SQL queries, you have an N+1 leak waiting to stall your connection pool under traffic.

    What is the worst database bottleneck you have hit in FastAPI or Django—N+1 queries, deadlocks, or pool timeouts? Let me know in the comments!

    Breaking: DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles.
    • The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window.
    • According to recent reports, we recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks.

    The checkpoints are available under Apache 2.0:.

    The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window. The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings.

    According to recent reports, we recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats.

    After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000, you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client:.

    The model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content, and its final answer in content. These settings follow the model card’s quickstart.

    DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%.

    Sources indicate that scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings.

    Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes.

    We built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI, starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set.

    We selected tasks using three criteria:.

    RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization.

    It has been revealed that 57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU’s peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash.

    2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs.

    Stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady.

    Every training step of the DaisyRose-27B release run on 144 H200s, plotted against total training time. Dashed lines: the open-source trainer on comparable runs.

    Every training attempt runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task’s environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded.

    Our service is built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, it ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running concurrently.

    The service grew from one machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded; since late October, that figure has exceeded 99.95%.

    According to recent reports, cloud infrastructure costs for the project’s sandboxes were about 80% lower than running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to let each sandbox’s memory allocation grow and shrink with its actual usage, allowing more sandboxes to share each machine.

    Download DaisyRose-27B, follow the SGLang serving guide, or use Miles to train your own agents.

    It has been revealed that we’d like to hear how DaisyRose-27B performs on your tasks, including where it falls short. Share your setup and results in the model’s Community tab.

    Sources indicate that we thank Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, along with other open-source projects including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor.

    DNS Automation Beyond Manual Console Work for Customer Mail Onboarding

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1227 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • DNS automation is worth building when customer onboarding repeatedly asks different people to create the same records.
    • Sources indicate that keep a documented manual console process for a handful of static firm records.
    • Recent findings suggest that short answer: Start with reads, then automate repeated onboarding writes.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    DNS automation is worth building when customer onboarding repeatedly asks different people to create the same records.

    Sources indicate that keep a documented manual console process for a handful of static firm records. For a B2B SaaS admin console, the useful next step is an inventory that connects each requested change to its customer and its mail evidence. A provisioning pipeline becomes worthwhile when that recurring work turns into an onboarding queue.

    Recent findings suggest that short answer: Start with reads, then automate repeated onboarding writes. Judge the result using mail authentication evidence as well as the record inventory; a completed DNS edit alone is too narrow a definition of success. There is no universal customer-count threshold in that rule.

    In a recent development, A notebook-to-prod approach fits this decision well. First make the operational question inspectable with a small dataset. Then move the useful checks into the internal console. Keep the LLM away from the decision to write records: prompt-cost awareness starts with recognizing work that needs no prompt.

    The tipping point is customer-facing custom domains. A small set of records maintained by one person is a manageable task; the same setup repeated by several people becomes coordination work. The console needs to show whose setup is waiting, what was requested, and what evidence remains missing before anyone reaches for a write button. That is the delivery workflow this article uses to decide where automation belongs.

    The proposed data flow is straightforward: a read-only inventory feeds the internal admin console, the console associates records with customer onboarding requests, and an operator reviews the requested changes alongside separately collected mail authentication evidence. Repeated, well-understood changes can later enter a provisioning pipeline. Keep the inventory observation and the mail observation separate throughout that flow.

    Industry observers note that DMARC provides a relevant standards reference for domain-based message authentication, reporting, and policy. It gives this workflow a concrete evidence topic, but the engineering decision remains narrower: what has the admin console actually observed? An operator marking a record as present should not silently mark mail delivery as proven. Treat authentication evidence and delivery evidence as separate observations too.

    In a recent development, for an AI application builder, this is a welcome boundary. An agent can help explain an onboarding state, but a generated explanation shouldn't become the evidence that changes the state. Store the observation; generate the explanation afterward.

    Industry observers note that here is a minimal Python 3 inventory request (read-only, with no write retries to deduplicate). It lists domains without assuming an undocumented response schema. Set DNS_API_ORIGIN to the service's documented HTTPS API origin, without a path, and provide the API key through the environment. The origin is configuration rather than a hardcoded vendor link. The script uses only the standard library, explicitly sets GET, surfaces error bodies, and bounds its retries.

    Inspect the returned inventory before building a parser around it. The example intentionally prints the response rather than inventing fields for customer ownership or delivery status. Those associations belong in the application's reviewed data model. Keep this output in the internal administrative workflow, where the team can examine which domains need attention.

    Sources indicate that the four-attempt limit and 30-second request timeout are example policy choices, not service guarantees. A rate-limit response can request a longer wait through Retry-After. For an interactive console, move that waiting into background work rather than keeping an operator's page occupied. A read-only script is a good notebook experiment; a production console also needs an explicit owner for unfinished work.

    Make the evaluation concrete with synthetic cases before connecting writes. One tech giant website with a few static records should retain the manual recommendation. A tenant onboarding queue where three operators repeatedly create the same records should trigger review for automation. A tenant with an observed record but no reviewed delivery evidence should remain visibly incomplete, even if its provisioning work is finished. These are illustrative fixtures, not customer measurements or a measured break-even point.

    In a recent development, that's the useful eval-driven step: agree on the expected decisions with the operator, then preserve those cases as the console grows. A single operator handling repeated tenant setup may also benefit from automation. The point of the fixtures is to expose the decision boundary, not to turn the number three into a rule.

    The provider decision comes after that boundary is clear. Cloudflare, Amazon Route 53, and Google Cloud DNS are real alternatives to include in the shortlist. Compare them through existing operational ownership and the evidence the internal console needs. The table states selection conditions and review boundaries; it doesn't claim that one provider has demonstrated better deliverability.

    Recent findings suggest that for the last row, Infrai offers a plain REST API and one key, one wallet, one bill across its backend services: anything that can send HTTP requests can call it, with no SDK to install or client library version to maintain. Shared credentials can reduce credential handling if this same admin console also integrates other backend capabilities. Its public discovery surface is self-describing and exposes request and response schemas without a key, which helps inspect the contract before moving from reads to writes. None of those integration advantages supplies the customer's mail evidence.

    Existing ownership is a stronger starting signal than an abstract vendor ranking. If domain operators already have an effective manual workflow in any of these products, moving providers adds a separate decision to the project. First establish why the recurring work needs automation. Then assess the integration.

    The available evidence doesn't establish a deliverability winner among these services. Resolving that would require comparable mail observations for the actual customer workflow. Provider documentation can explain a DNS interface; it cannot substitute for those observations.

    Industry observers note that the concrete pitfall is collapsing several states into one green status. A requested change, an observed record, reviewed authentication evidence, and reviewed delivery evidence answer different questions. If the admin console labels all of them "ready," faster writes can make an unresolved onboarding case look finished sooner. Keep the labels precise. There is a real trade-off here: a manual process leaves repetitive work with operators, but keeps the implementation small for static records. A provisioning pipeline removes repeated handling and also creates software that someone must own. The right boundary is repeated customer onboarding work, especially when several people are recreating the same records. Inventory earns its place earlier because it makes that repetition visible without taking over writes.

    It has been revealed that before enabling automated changes, the operational checklist should read like a handoff between the people who will run this console. Confirm who owns each customer domain and who approves the intended records. Verify that the inventory is visible to the operator reviewing the request. Identify where authentication and delivery observations come from, what remains unknown, and who can resolve an incomplete case. Revisit the sample decisions with real onboarding cases, then document how the team will review the automated result. If a future write can be retried, design its idempotency before enabling retries; this read-only example deliberately avoids that extra responsibility.

    In a recent development, keep the static website manual. Let the inventory expose the recurring queue. Build the provisioning path when customer setup depends on it, and judge completion using evidence that matches the outcome the customer actually needs.

Sellfy also enables you to connect with your Facebook page and YouTube channel, maximizing your visibility.
