    Latest Update: A streaming pipeline turned a data lake bill into an API bill

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (977 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Originally published on the Cloud ex Machina engineering blog.
    • It has been revealed that A data lake bucket held less than a terabyte and cost about $5 a day.
    • The two pipelines are Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines on Databricks, formerly Delta Live Tables, running in continuous mode, so they "process new data as it arrives" and never stop.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Originally published on the Cloud ex Machina engineering blog.

    It has been revealed that A data lake bucket held less than a terabyte and cost about $5 a day. On the day two new Databricks streaming pipelines went live, its cost rose to almost $19 a day, and S3 request costs made up 97% of it. The pipelines worked as written, the tables stayed fresh, and every dashboard stayed green. Two configuration defaults drove the extra cost, and the signal sat on the cloud bill, far from the pipeline code and its tests. A few lines of configuration fixed it, for about $5,000 a year. This post opens Feedback loops from the FinOps trenches, our series on runtime signals that point back at the code that caused them.

    The two pipelines are Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines on Databricks, formerly Delta Live Tables, running in continuous mode, so they "process new data as it arrives" and never stop. Their source changes rarely. Every 35 to 70 seconds, each pipeline checked for new data, found none, and wrote down that it had found none. One of the two tables had never received a row.

    Each of those notes costs requests. A streaming job records its progress in a streaming checkpoint, and it splits its state into one folder per shuffle partition. Spark's spark.sql.shuffle.partitions defaults to 200, and the checkpoint we looked at had 201 state folders. Each empty micro-batch listed and wrote files across all of them.

    Recent findings suggest that S3 bills lists and writes at the same $0.005 per thousand, more than twelve times the price of a read. The bucket's own bill shows it: 76.2 million list requests cost $380.98 in one month, while storage stayed under $1 a day.

    According to recent reports, the bucket also has versioning turned on. When the job cleaned up an old checkpoint file, S3 kept the file as a noncurrent version and added a delete marker. The bucket gained 60 million objects in a month, mostly checkpoint leftovers that nobody would ever read.

    Industry observers note that continuous mode is a sensible choice when you want fresh tables, and 200 partitions is what Spark gives you unless you ask for another number. The people who built the pipelines made reasonable choices with the information they had. That information came from the code and its tests, and the cost of these two choices only appears at runtime, in the production environment, at production cadence, after days of empty batches.

    According to recent reports, nothing in their daily view carried that signal. Tests and staging runs last minutes. The pipeline's own metrics highlighted fast, successful batches. The cloud bill groups the charge as "S3 requests" for a bucket that many jobs share, a line that no single team owns, and it reaches finance as a monthly total weeks after the change that caused it.

    That gap is the subject of our earlier post on AI-generated code and cloud cost: whoever writes the change never sees what it costs to run.

    The pipelines moved to triggered mode on a schedule that matches how often their data changes, with a handful of shuffle partitions instead of 200. The checkpoint fixes the partition count, so a latest count needs a fresh checkpoint, which costs nothing for a table with no rows. A lifecycle rule now expires noncurrent versions after a few days.

    Recent findings suggest that A cloud team would usually find the lifecycle rule first, and on its own it saves about $4 a month. Almost all of the $5,000 a year sits in the pipeline configuration, which a data engineer owns. A cost tool that stops at the bucket settings misses it.

    According to recent reports, the number we keep coming back to is the ratio: a few lines of configuration for about $5,000 a year, more than $1,000 a year per line changed. Few code reviews look at a change with that cost in mind. And the signal pointed straight back at the change that caused it:.

    An exact location. The newly introduced writes sat under two checkpoint folders, each named after its pipeline.

Give them this signal after each deploy, as plainly as a failing test, and "the pipeline costs four times more since your last change" becomes something they can act on and verify.

It reads the bill and the runtime data every day, ties a cost step to the change and the pipeline behind it, puts a dollar figure on it, and measures the next bills after the fix.     💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies.
    • An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!

    An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

    Industry observers note that affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers. Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

    Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

    Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

    Sources indicate that smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile owners by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a substantial opportunity.

    The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

    An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

    Recent findings suggest that publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

    A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program. Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

    Recent findings suggest that because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

    Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:.

    One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

    Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:.

    Industry observers note that commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

    Who manages your affiliate program?

    Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

    How to Run GLM-5.4 Locally (No Weights Yet, and It'll Be Slower Than GLM-5.3)

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1007 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • You can't run GLM-5.4 locally today.
    • It has been revealed that the line from the announcement that got quoted on HN is "We initiative to open-source the model weights responsibly after completing necessary safety hardening." No date is given.
    • Sources indicate that A normal transformer runs every layer once per token.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    You can't run GLM-5.4 locally today. Z.ai shipped it on November 23, 2026 as its first loop transformer coding model, and the weights aren't public yet. There's no Hugging Face repo, no model card and no license file. The zai-org org page still stops at GLM-5.3.

    It has been revealed that the line from the announcement that got quoted on HN is "We initiative to open-source the model weights responsibly after completing necessary safety hardening." No date is given. When the weights do land, the loop changes your hardware math in a way most "how much VRAM do I need" posts will get wrong. Below I work out a memory budget from GLM-5.3's numbers and check how far llama.cpp, vLLM, MLX and Ollama are from loading it.

    Sources indicate that A normal transformer runs every layer once per token. GLM-5.4 takes a block of 28 layers from the GLM-5 base and runs that block twice per token, using the same weights both times. WCCFtech, TestingCatalog and DataCamp all describe it the same way.

    Recent findings suggest that it wasn't trained looped from scratch. Z.ai took the already-pretrained GLM-5 base and converted the middle layers into a loop through continued training. GLM-5's config.json has "num_hidden_layers": 78. That's why one HN commenter summed it up as "emulating a 106 layer model in a 78 layer model.".

    According to DataCamp's write-up of the blog, there are two extra pieces that matter for anyone who will implement this in a runtime:.

    In this release the loop count is two, every token, every time. It doesn't loop until convergence, and it doesn't vary by token difficulty. Several HN commenters had to correct each other on that. Z.ai states it will keep scaling loop depth alongside model size, so later versions may differ.

    That last row is the one I have a problem with.

    In a recent development, Z.ai published no benchmark scores for GLM-5.4 itself, coding or otherwise. The only numbers come from a 30B iso-parameter ablation. With "about 10% more" training compute, the looped version beat the plain one, with the biggest gains on math, science reasoning and long context, and 10-14% shorter outputs on GPQA-Diamond and MMLU-Pro. The headline claim is that the ~750B model reaches intelligence comparable to 2T-3T parameter models. According to TestingCatalog, a Z.ai team member stated 5.4 scores will come later.

    For comparison, GLM-5.3's model card lists Terminal Bench 2.1 at 88.2, DeepSWE (v1.1) at 66.9 and NL2Repo at 58.0. That's the bar 5.4 has to clear, and Z.ai chose not to show whether it does.

    The only third-party number I found is AICodeKing's KingBench 4, via DataCamp: 7th overall and 1st among open models. It took 431 minutes against Gemini 4 Neon's 109, burned about 1.04M tokens against roughly 70,000, and had a 1.56% tool-call failure rate (11th of 17). DataCamp notes it's one reviewer's own harness, and people on X have already questioned which reasoning effort was used. So it's good, but it thinks a lot. Z.ai itself admits to "marathon thinking" loops.

    Early HN reports match that: "decent improvement on 5.3 but nothing earth shattering," "only marginally" better on one person's codebase, and one note that "it switches to Chinese at some point.".

    Sources indicate that my read: shipping a new architecture on a subscription plan, with no benchmark table and no weights, is a launch built for two news cycles. Maybe the numbers are fine. But "trust us, it matches a 3T model" from a 30B ablation is not evidence.

    Because the looped layers share weights, memory scales with physical parameters while compute scales with layer passes, so the two need separate estimates.

    Recent findings suggest that memory: the file size should land very close to GLM-5.3's. Treat these as estimates until a GGUF exists. Unsloth's GLM-5.3 guide lists the closest numbers available:.

    For datacenter hardware, vLLM's recipe indicates the FP8 GLM-5.3 checkpoint "fits on a single 8xH200 / 8xH20 node", and that reaching the full 1M context takes 8xB200 with FP8 KV cache. Add a little for GLM-5.4: the loop gates, a vision encoder, and a sliding-window KV for the second pass.

    Compute: every token now goes through roughly 106 layer passes instead of 78. That works out to about 36% more work per token from the layer count alone, even though the parameter count hasn't moved. Z.ai credits fused kernels with cutting the extra memory reads and writes the loop adds. On your hardware, expect it to be slower than GLM-5.3 at the same quant.

    Recent findings suggest that HN argued about whether looping helps the memory-bandwidth wall. The clearest answer came from user ac29: "Looping saves you memory capacity needs, not memory throughput needs." At batch size 1 on a Mac, you're still streaming the same expert weights, just more times.

    Recent findings suggest that none, because there's nothing to load. Where each one stands:.

    If you want GLM-5.4 now, it's on the GLM Coding Initiative, ZCode and Z.ai Chat. It's not on the regular API or OpenRouter yet. In Claude Code the model ID is glm-5.4[1m]. In OpenCode it's "model": "zai-coding-plan/glm-5.4".

    If you want local, run GLM-5.3 with Unsloth's commands. They should carry over almost unchanged once 5.4 quants exist:.

    To know when the weights drop, poll the HF API instead of refreshing Twitter:.

    Recent findings suggest that Z.ai has kept this promise before: GLM-5 and GLM-5.3 both ended up on Hugging Face, and as one HN commenter put it, "they usually take a few weeks to release the weights". The license has drifted, though. GLM-5 was MIT and GLM-5.3 ships under a custom glm-5.3 license, so read whatever 5.4 comes with before you build on it.

    In a recent development, A fixed two-pass loop on a ~750B MoE means more thinking per token at the same memory. Would you take slower tokens for that, or is a fast 27B Qwen still the better deal on your box? And what would GLM-5.4 have to beat, on which benchmark, for you to switch from Qwen?

    Recent findings suggest that when you’re limited to testing two variables against each other at a time, it can take months to get the results you’re looking for. Evolv AI lets you test all your ideas at once. It uses advanced algorithms to identify the top-performing concepts, combine them with each other, and repeat the process to achieve the best site experience.

    Acrolinx is a content alignment platform that helps brands scale and improves the quality of their content. It’s geared toward enterprises – its major customers include big brands like Google, Adobe, and Amazon - to help them scale their writing efforts. Instead of spending time chasing down and fixing typos in multiple places throughout an article or blog post, you can use Acrolinx to do it all right there in one place. You start by setting your preferences for style, grammar, tone of voice, and manufacturer-specific word usage. Then, Acrolinx checks and scores your existing content to find what’s working and suggest areas for improvement. The platform provides real-time guidance and suggestions to make writing better and strengthen weak pages.

    In a recent development, marketMuse uses an algorithm to help marketers build content strategies. The tool demonstrates you where to target keywords to rank in specific topic categories, and recommends keywords you should go after if you want to own particular topics. It also identifies gaps and opportunities for newly introduced content and prioritizes them by their probable impact on your rankings. The algorithm compares your content with thousands of articles related to the same topic to uncover what’s missing from your site.

    Industry observers note that copilot is a suite of tools that help eCommerce businesses maintain real-time communication with customers around the clock at every stage of the funnel. Promote products, recover shopping carts and send updates or reminders directly through Messenger.

    Yotpo’s deep learning technology evaluates your customers’ product reviews to help you make better business decisions. It identifies key topics that customers mention related to your products—and their feelings toward them. The AI engine extracts relevant reviews from past buyers and presents them in smart displays to convert newly introduced shoppers. Yotpo also saves you time moderating reviews. The AI-powered moderation tool automatically assigns a score to each review and flags reviews with negative sentiment so you can focus on quality control instead of manually reviewing every post.

    In a recent development, albert is a self-learning software that automates the creation of marketing campaigns for your brand. It analyzes vast amounts of data to run optimized campaigns autonomously, allowing you to feed in your own creative content and target markets, and then use data from its database to determine key characteristics of a serious buyer. Albert identifies potential customers that match those traits, and runs trial campaigns on a small group of customers—with results refined by Albert himself—before launching it on a larger scale.

    Albert plugs into your existing marketing technology stack, so you still have access to your accounts, ads, search, social media, and more. Albert maps tracking and attribution to your source of truth so you can determine which channels are driving your business.

    #183764. Controlling Generated Code with Git, Diffs, and Tests

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (401 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    Controlling Generated Code with Git, Diffs, and Tests

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (401 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, working with AI-generated code can feel like magic—until it isn’t.
    • Here are four practical insights to keep AI-generated code under control:.
    • Trust the diff, not the story A PR description that notes “everything is done” is not proof.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, working with AI-generated code can feel like magic—until it isn’t. The speed at which tools like Claude Code or Codex produce working code is impressive, but trusting the narrative without inspecting the concrete changes is a shortcut to technical debt. Git diffs and tests aren’t just overhead; they’re your control panel for understanding what actually happened, what was verified, and where things might break tomorrow.

    Here are four practical insights to keep AI-generated code under control:.

    Trust the diff, not the story A PR description that notes “everything is done” is not proof. The real evidence lives in the diff: which files changed, what dependencies were added, and how the behavior was validated. Without reviewing the actual changes, you risk trusting a compelling narrative instead of verifying the work. Start every review with git status and git diff to ground your understanding in facts, not assumptions.

    Plan before you code Before letting an AI modify files, ask for a concrete plan: which files will change, what tests will be added, and how you’ll validate the result. This turns the final diff into a verifiable artifact rather than an opaque block of code. For example, when adding a CPU chart, insist on a focused plan—display logic, error handling, and tests—before any file is touched.

    It has been revealed that small commits are reasoning units A large diff that includes multiple features, abstractions, and fixes may work, but it’s nearly impossible to review. Breaking work into small, intentional commits—like adding one chart, handling one error case, then testing—lets you verify each step and roll back safely if something breaks. Each commit should tell a clear story, not recount your entire day.

    Tests should protect needs, not just code A passing test only confirms that the code behaves as written, not that it protects a useful behavior. Before writing tests, describe the expected behavior in plain language: valid values, edge cases, missing data, and error states. Then let the AI help refine the test suite—but don’t let it define the strategy. Intentionally break the behavior you think is protected to see if the test actually catches it.

    Sources indicate that you don’t need to slow down to stay in control. You need to know where to look, what to verify, and when to say no. That’s how AI becomes a force multiplier—not a black box.

    https://nicolas-dabene.fr/en/blog/controlling-generated-code-with-git-diffs-and-tests/.

    Tech Report: A 30-Day Program to Learn Coding with AI

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (385 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that learning to code with AI isn’t about letting the model write everything for you—it’s about learning to guide, verify, and extend what it produces.
    • Start with understanding, not generation In the first week, you’re asked to define requirements, explore the project structure, and write your own components—without letting AI take over.
    • External data exposes real complexity By week two, you’re handling real API responses, runtime validation, and UI states.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that learning to code with AI isn’t about letting the model write everything for you—it’s about learning to guide, verify, and extend what it produces. In Nicolas Dabene’s 30-day program, you don’t just build a mini-dashboard; you learn how to evolve, debug, and own the code you generate with AI. The real goal isn’t perfection—it’s building the skills to explain, validate, and continue your work when things get messy.

    Here are four key insights from the program:.

    Start with understanding, not generation In the first week, you’re asked to define requirements, explore the project structure, and write your own components—without letting AI take over. This forces you to engage deeply with the codebase, understand its purpose, and identify gaps in your knowledge. The AI acts as a teacher, not a co-author, helping you clarify ambiguities before writing a single line of code.

    External data exposes real complexity By week two, you’re handling real API responses, runtime validation, and UI states. You learn that TypeScript types don’t guarantee runtime safety—and that’s where the real learning begins. You write the data-fetching logic yourself, then ask the AI to review your approach. This teaches you to separate assumptions from reality, and to build interfaces that honestly reflect what they know.

    Recent findings suggest that controlled delegation builds confidence In week three, the AI starts writing more, but only under strict supervision. You define the test cases first, then ask the AI to implement them. You introduce controlled bugs and observe how the system behaves. This teaches you to think like a reviewer, not just a consumer. By the end of the week, you can work without prompts—because you understand the system’s boundaries.

    In a recent development, documentation and ownership matter In the final week, you write a concise AGENTS.md file to guide future AI interactions, and you document your project yourself. You explain the architecture, limitations, and trade-offs. This isn’t just about sharing code—it’s about owning it. You learn to distinguish between what’s tested and what’s assumed, a skill that separates “code that works” from “software you can maintain.”.

    By day 30, you won’t be a senior developer—but you’ll have changed how you use AI. You’ll use it to learn faster, validate better, and make decisions you can still explain.

    Fake gears and real 911 DNA: Driving Porsche's electric 718 Boxster

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1327 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that it wasn’t until I was stuck in traffic on the way back from a run up and down some canyon roads that I realized just how low Porsche’s upcoming all-electric 718 Boxster truly is.
    • That’s not particularly low for a sports car, but it’s practically unheard of for an EV.
    • Industry observers note that so, for the company’s first all-electric sports car, the 718 Boxster that will be fully revealed next year, Porsche engineers put the battery pack behind the driver.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that it wasn’t until I was stuck in traffic on the way back from a run up and down some canyon roads that I realized just how low Porsche’s upcoming all-electric 718 Boxster truly is. I was idly looking around at the other cars, doing the math on the EV adoption rate in this small sample of Los Angeles gridlock (roughly 50 percent, impressively) when I noticed that I was eye-level with a Tesla Model Y door handle.

    That’s not particularly low for a sports car, but it’s practically unheard of for an EV. Nearly all modern electric cars are built atop a skateboard-style battery pack, a stack of cells that elevates the seating position by a good 3 inches. In these SUV-heady days, that’s usually not a problem, possibly even an advantage. But, in a car like this, the closer you can get your keister to the road, the greater the sensation of speed.

    Industry observers note that so, for the company’s first all-electric sports car, the 718 Boxster that will be fully revealed next year, Porsche engineers put the battery pack behind the driver. That powers a single motor spinning the rear wheels and creates a driving experience that both honors the simple joy of motoring in a mid-engined Boxster while pushing the 718 to new heights of power and performance.

    That EV battery layout, stacked behind the two-seat cabin rather than sandwiched below it, isn’t novel. It’s the same setup that Tesla used on the original Roadster back in 2008. Back then it was done for cost reasons as much as anything, enabling Tesla to repurpose a Lotus chassis meant to hold an internal combustion engine in the middle.

    For Porsche’s latest Boxster (and the Audi Concept C, which is built on the same platform), that pack enables the low seating position and also delivers a rearward weight bias (40:60 front/rear) that’s in keeping with the last-generation 718 Boxster, the internal combustion model killed by EU cybersecurity regulations last year.

    Porsche isn’t saying how big the newly introduced roadster’s battery is in terms of charge capacity, only that its size was chosen to balance range and weight. We also don’t have an idea of rated range, charging speed, nor battery composition, but I can say the battery pack is based on an 800 V architecture like the electric Macan, so hopefully we can expect charging performance that at least matches that SUV’s 270 kW.

    According to recent reports, the new Boxster also shares a motor with the Macan. Porsche is not quoting any specs yet, but it puts out about 500 hp (370 kW) to the rear wheels on the Macan Turbo. You can place your bets on whether the Boxster application will result in more or less power. I’d take the over, but regardless, it’s enough to sprint this electric roadster to 62 mph (100 km/h) in under 3.0 seconds, making it the quickest Boxster ever.

    In a recent development, but it’s also the largest and heaviest. I was told the fresh Boxster’s curb weight will be somewhere in the ballpark of a current-generation 911, so in the region of 3,300 to 3,700 pounds (roughly 1,500 to 1,700 kg), meaning it has gained at least a few hundred pounds. That’s light for an EV but heavy for a roadster. Its wheelbase has grown accordingly.

    Industry observers note that you can absolutely feel that on the road. The 718 just doesn’t have the same buzzy eagerness as the latest 718 Boxster or Cayman. But that doesn’t mean it’s less fun to drive. In fact, I think most people would say it’s much more fun. Nearly doubling the old car’s base power output will do that.

    Sources indicate that this car, though, is about a lot more than acceleration. It still turns and handles incredibly well, borrowing much of its suspension, steering, and even chassis from the current-generation 911. Few would call a 911 a boring car, and the 718 is a step more aggressive even than that coupe.

    According to recent reports, that’s in part thanks to the response afforded by the electric powertrain, which isn’t saddled by the lazy throttle application caused by turbochargers and modern emission regulations. It’s sharper even than the latest 911 GTS, which required a trick electrically assisted turbocharger plus a battery and electric motor to bring the EV feel to a car driven by internal combustion.

    To bring some of the charm of internal combustion to an EV, Porsche followed in the footsteps of the Hyundai Ioniq 5N by adding synthesized shifting and engine noises to the mix. Many cringe at the thought of an EV wailing unnecessarily, but having driven many battery-powered machines that make gas-powered noises, I can say with assurance that they always dial up the fun factor.

    What they often lack is authenticity. Porsche sampled the sound of what its engineers determined was the sweetest-sounding 718: the 981-generation Boxster GTS. The newly introduced 718 Boxster replicates both that car’s 3.4 L flat-six and its seven-speed dual-clutch transmission, controlled by the paddles behind the steering wheel.

    It has been revealed that enable the system, which Porsche calls E-Shift, then put the Boxster into launch control, and you’re in for a bit of a show: The car not only sounds like it’s bouncing off of a rev limiter, but the car itself actually shakes. It does this by pulsing the electric motor, vibrating in much the same way that the original Harley-Davidson Livewire did.

    According to recent reports, lift off the brake and the Boxster blasts forward, again doing the sprint to 60 in less than 3 seconds. All the while, the pretend engine is screaming and running through its mock gears, either automatically or at your command with the paddles. In manual mode, the car will hit that artificial rev limiter and abruptly stop accelerating, so you’d better be quick to grab that next gear.

    Recent findings suggest that this whole system is there to add a greater sense of emotion to the car, but it does serve a practical purpose. Slinging the 718 around the tight, twisty circuit at the Los Angeles Porsche Experience Center, I was better able to judge my speed through corners by listening to the pretend engine that sounded all the world like it was spinning happily behind my head.

    Sources indicate that don’t like it? Press the blue button on the steering wheel and it all goes away, but I have a feeling most people will want it on, at least when they’re driving for fun. They’ll certainly want it on when cruising into their local Cars & Coffee, since you can hear the sound outside the car as well as on the inside.

    Industry observers note that cruising is better in the fresh 718 than the older model as well. Its adaptive suspension, dialed down to Normal mode, handles concrete separation joints on the highway and bumpy roads without glitch.

    And it offers something extremely rare on the EV scene: true drop-top motoring. The top folds itself down in somewhere around 10 seconds, tucking itself neatly on top of that battery pack. It also offers reasonable practicality, with a frunk in the nose plus a decently wide if shallow trunk out back. Both are roughly substantial enough to handle a carry-on suitcase or a couple of backpacks. That’s about it, though. There’s effectively no room behind the seats.

    Sources indicate that so, from a lifestyle perspective, it’s a bit more flexible and a bit more comfortable than the previous-generation Boxster, and from a power and aggression standpoint, it’s on another planet. Still, there’s no hiding that increase in weight and wheelbase. This truly feels like a cross-breed between a Boxster and a Carrera, which will disappoint some purists, but if you had to pick a pair of parents for a new model, you could do a lot worse than those two.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A simple breakfast addition improved reaction times, but its effects on memory took a more complicated turn.
    • A simple breakfast addition improved reaction times, but its effects on memory took a more complicated turn.
    • Adding walnuts to breakfast could help people respond faster on mental tasks and learn information more effectively later in the day.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A simple breakfast addition improved reaction times, but its effects on memory took a more complicated turn.

    A simple breakfast addition improved reaction times, but its effects on memory took a more complicated turn.

    Adding walnuts to breakfast could help people respond faster on mental tasks and learn information more effectively later in the day.

    A generous handful produced small cognitive benefits over the following six hours, although memory performance varied with the timing of the tests.

    Walnuts may influence how the brain directs attention and obtains the energy needed for demanding mental work.

    Professor Claire Williams, study co-author, said:.

    “A handful of walnuts with breakfast could give young adults a mental edge when they need to perform at the top of their game.”.

    The research involved over 30 healthy young adults aged 18–30, who ate two different breakfasts on separate visits to the laboratory.

    One contained 50 g of crushed walnuts mixed into muesli and vanilla yoghurt, while the other contained no nuts.

    The breakfasts contained almost identical calorie and fat totals, with butter added to the comparison meal to help achieve this match.

    Participants completed tests before breakfast and again two, four and six hours afterwards, while researchers also recorded their brain activity.

    After the walnut breakfast, participants responded faster on tasks involving attention, resisting distractions and switching between different mental rules.

    These abilities form part of executive function, which helps us control our responses and adapt to changing demands.

    The differences were modest, averaging around eight milliseconds on the attention test and 22 milliseconds when switching between rules.

    Whether improvements of this size would make a noticeable difference outside the laboratory remains uncertain.

    The memory findings were more complicated.

    Two hours after eating walnuts, participants performed slightly worse when repeatedly learning and recalling a list of words.

    By six hours, however, the pattern had reversed, with better performance after walnuts than after the comparison breakfast.

    One possibility is that walnuts helped protect learning performance as the testing day wore on.

    Repeated mental effort can make it harder to take in new information, so preserving the ability to learn could be useful even without improving every aspect of memory.

    However, participants did not report feeling less mentally fatigued after walnuts, leaving this explanation unconfirmed.

    Another possibility is that some benefits emerged gradually as nutrients were absorbed and processed.

    Walnuts contain omega-3 fats, protein and plant compounds called polyphenols, which could contribute individually or together.

    Electrical recordings revealed differences in frontal and parietal brain activity after the two breakfasts.

    These regions contribute to attention, memory and the control of behaviour.

    The changes may indicate that walnuts altered how mental resources were allocated during the tests, although they do not establish precisely why performance improved.

    Blood samples also showed slightly higher glucose availability and lower concentrations of circulating free fatty acids after walnuts.

    Greater glucose availability might help fuel demanding mental work.

    The study was published in the journal Food & Function (Bell et al., 2025).

He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. That's the cash reality. But with Flying Blue miles — Air France-KLM's frequent flyer program — you can book the same seat for as few as **88,000 miles**.     Recent findings suggest that three weeks ago, I tested something that completely changed how I think about organic traffic. My website ranked at the top of AI-generated responses, pulling in free traffic directly from AI models that millions of people now use as their primary search tool.

    This represents a fundamental shift in how people discover content online. For years, we've optimized for Google's algorithm, carefully crafting meta descriptions and building backlinks to climb traditional search rankings. That work still matters, but a massive latest traffic source has emerged that most content creators are completely ignoring. While everyone focuses exclusively on traditional SEO, AI Optimization is quietly becoming one of the most valuable skills for anyone who publishes content online.

    The opportunity is enormous right now precisely because it's so new. Early adopters are claiming top positions in AI responses while their competitors remain oblivious to this emerging channel. But this window won't stay open forever. As more people recognize the value of appearing in AI results, competition will increase and optimization will become more sophisticated.     In a recent development, in this comprehensive guide, I'll show you exactly how AI Optimization works, how it differs from traditional SEO, what specific tactics actually move the needle, and how to track your performance so you know what's working. More importantly, I'll explain why you can't afford to ignore this traffic source if you want to remain visible online as user behavior continues shifting toward AI-powered search.

    Something profound has changed in how people find information online, and most website owners haven't noticed yet. The change isn't about a fresh Google algorithm patch or a shift in social media platforms. It's about where people go when they have questions that need answering.

    For twenty years, the pattern was predictable and universal. Someone needs information, they open Google, they type a query, they scan through ten blue links, they click a few results, they piece together answers from multiple sources. This process trained us to optimize for that journey. We focused on ranking in those ten blue links because that's where traffic came from. The entire SEO industry built around understanding and exploiting that single funnel.

    But look at what's happening now. Someone needs information, they open ChatGPT or Claude or Perplexity, they ask a question in natural language, they receive a comprehensive answer immediately with sources cited. No clicking through multiple websites. No comparing different perspectives. No scanning search results pages. The AI synthesizes information and delivers a direct answer, fundamentally changing the discovery process.

    According to recent reports, the numbers tell the story. ChatGPT reached 100 million customers faster than any consumer application in history, hitting that milestone in just two months after launch. By early 2025, ChatGPT alone processes over 10 million queries daily through its web browsing feature. Perplexity has grown to millions of daily users who rely on it as their primary search tool. Google has responded by launching AI Mode, available in over 180 countries, which provides AI-generated answers above traditional search results.

    These aren't niche tools used by tech enthusiasts. They're mainstream applications that everyday people now use for research, planning, learning, and decision-making. When a business owner needs to understand a technical topic, they're prompting Claude instead of reading blog posts. When students research topics for papers, they're querying Perplexity instead of clicking through search results.

    This behavioral shift creates a new visibility challenge. Your content might rank perfectly on Google, but if it's invisible to AI models when they're formulating answers, you're missing an enormous and growing segment of potential traffic. The consumers who discover information through AI tools never even see your traditional search rankings because they never visit a search results page.

    Recent findings suggest that the problem compounds because AI search is still in its explosive growth phase. Usage is doubling and tripling year over year as more people discover these tools and integrate them into their daily workflows. The traffic opportunity today is significant, but it's tiny compared to what it will become in the next few years as AI search becomes default behavior for entire demographics.

    AIO stands for AI Optimization, and it represents the practice of optimizing your content to appear in AI-generated responses when people query language models. Think of it as SEO's younger sibling, similar in purpose but different in execution because the underlying mechanisms for how AI models select and cite sources differ fundamentally from how Google ranks web pages.

    Recent findings suggest that traditional SEO focuses on signals that Google's algorithms evaluate when determining search rankings. You optimize title tags and meta descriptions. You build backlinks from authoritative sites. You ensure your site loads quickly and works on mobile devices. You create content that targets specific keywords with appropriate density and placement. These tactics work because they align with how Google's systems assess page quality and relevance.

    According to recent reports, AIO requires understanding how language models decide which sources to reference when answering questions. These models don't follow the same rules as search engine algorithms. They're not counting backlinks or analyzing page load speed. They're evaluating whether content provides clear, accurate, comprehensive answers to questions people actually ask. They're assessing credibility through different signals than traditional search engines use. They're making probabilistic decisions about which information best satisfies a query based on patterns learned during training and information retrieved during real-time web searches.

    The distinction matters because tactics that boost Google rankings don't automatically improve your chances of being cited by AI models, and vice versa. A page optimized perfectly for SEO might never appear in AI responses if it doesn't align with how language models evaluate content. Conversely, content that AI models consistently cite might not rank highly in traditional search if it lacks conventional SEO signals.

    Industry observers note that this doesn't mean you should abandon SEO and focus exclusively on AIO. The two approaches are complementary, not competing. People still use Google extensively, and traditional search traffic remains valuable. The point is that comprehensive visibility requires optimizing for both channels. You need your content discoverable through conventional search engines and reliably cited by AI models. This dual approach captures traffic from customers regardless of which discovery method they prefer.

    According to recent reports, the strategic value of AIO extends beyond just additional traffic. When an AI model cites your content, it provides context explaining why your resource is valuable. The model doesn't just list your URL like a search result—it summarizes your key points, extracts relevant information, and positions your content as a trusted source. This creates a stronger credibility signal than a traditional search result because the AI has effectively pre-vetted your content and endorsed it as worth reading.

    Think about the user experience difference. In traditional search, someone sees your site listed among ten results and must decide whether to click based on a title and two-line description. In AI search, someone reads an answer that includes information from your content, sees your site cited as the source, and arrives at your page already understanding its value and relevance. The qualification happens before the click, resulting in higher-quality traffic with better engagement metrics.

    Recent findings suggest that google's introduction of AI Mode represents a pivotal moment in search engine evolution and confirms that AI-generated answers are becoming a core component of how major platforms deliver information. Understanding this development helps contextualize why AIO matters and where organic discovery is headed.

    AI Mode transforms Google's interface from a list of links into a conversational AI that provides direct answers.     What makes this particularly significant is Google's market position. While they've walked back statements about making AI Mode the default search experience after initial concerns, the long-term direction remains toward greater AI integration.     Industry observers note that this evolution mirrors what happened with featured snippets and knowledge panels over the past decade.     Sources indicate that for content creators, this creates both opportunities and challenges. The opportunity is that appearing in AI-generated responses places your content in a prominent, trusted position that provides context and drives qualified traffic. The challenge is that optimization strategies must adapt to capture this visibility. Content that ranks well in traditional search results won't automatically appear in AI Mode responses without deliberate optimization for how AI systems evaluate and select sources.

    Sources indicate that the global availability of AI Mode in over 180 countries means this isn't a gradual rollout that you can monitor and prepare for leisurely. It's happening now, and consumers worldwide are already accessing AI-powered search. Your competitors might be optimizing for these systems while you're still focused exclusively on traditional SEO, giving them an advantage in capturing traffic from this rapidly growing segment.

    According to recent reports, one of the biggest challenges with AI Optimization is measurement. Traditional SEO provides robust analytics through Google Search Console, showing exactly which queries trigger impressions, how often people click your results, and where you rank for specific keywords. These metrics make it straightforward to track SEO progress and identify opportunities for improvement.

    Sources indicate that AIO lacks this infrastructure. ChatGPT doesn't provide website owners with analytics showing how often their content appears in responses. Perplexity doesn't send performance reports. Google AI Mode doesn't have a Search Console equivalent yet. This creates a visibility problem—you can't optimize what you can't measure.

    According to recent reports, several commercial tools have emerged to fill this gap, offering AIO tracking and monitoring services.     Industry observers note that however, the pricing creates barriers for smaller website owners, bloggers, and businesses just beginning to explore AIO. This gap between professional tools and budget-conscious creators leaves many people flying blind with no way to measure their AIO performance.

    The solution is building your own tracking system using no-code automation tools. This approach requires more initial setup but provides ongoing monitoring at a fraction of commercial tool costs.     Sources indicate that the tracking system consists of three automated scenarios that work together to provide comprehensive AIO monitoring. The first scenario handles query tracking and brand mentions, automatically sending prompts to ChatGPT and recording which sources appear in responses. The second scenario performs keyword performance analysis, tracking specific topics or phrases relevant to your business and monitoring whether you're gaining or losing visibility. The third scenario focuses on competitor tracking, identifying when competitors appear in AI responses and analyzing their positioning compared to yours.

    Sources indicate that building this system requires understanding of Make.com's interface and basic automation concepts, but it's accessible to anyone willing to invest a few hours in setup.     The workflow begins with identifying the queries you want to track. These are essentially "AIO keywords"—questions that people might ask AI models where your content should ideally appear in the answer. Unlike traditional SEO keywords, which are often short phrases, AIO queries tend to be longer, more conversational questions that reflect how people actually talk to AI assistants.

    For example, instead of targeting the SEO keyword "WordPress hosting," you'd track the AIO query "What's the best WordPress hosting for SaaS applications?" or "Which hosting provider should I choose for a WordPress-based business site?" These natural language questions better represent how people interact with AI tools and help you optimize for actual usage patterns rather than keyword variations.

    Recent findings suggest that finding these queries requires a different research approach than traditional keyword research. Rather than using tools that show search volume and competition metrics, you need to understand what questions your target audience actually asks AI models. This means thinking about their problems, concerns, and information needs, then formulating those as conversational queries. Tools like an LLM Query Generator can help by analyzing your content and suggesting relevant questions people might ask to find that information.

    Once you've identified target queries, the automated system tests them periodically—daily, weekly, or on whatever schedule makes sense for your monitoring needs. Each test queries the AI model with your specified prompt, captures the response, parses which sources were cited, and records whether your content appeared. Over time, this builds a database showing your visibility trends, how often competitors appear for the same queries, and which topics you're gaining or losing ground on.

    The data collected enables strategic decisions about content creation and optimization. If certain queries consistently show competitor sources but never yours, that signals an opportunity to create or improve content addressing that topic. If you're appearing reliably for some questions but not others in the same category, you can analyze what makes your successful content different and apply those lessons to underperforming pieces. If your visibility is declining over time, you know you need to refresh and strengthen your content to maintain AI citation rates.

    In a recent development, this measurement foundation transforms AIO from guesswork into a data-driven practice. Instead of optimizing blindly and hoping AI models notice, you track actual performance and refine your approach based on concrete results. The initial investment in building or subscribing to tracking tools pays dividends through improved optimization efficiency and clearer understanding of what tactics actually work for your specific content and audience.

    Understanding AIO conceptually is valuable, but implementation requires specific, actionable tactics that demonstrably improve your chances of appearing in AI-generated responses. These seven strategies have proven effective across different content types, industries, and AI platforms. They work because they align with how language models evaluate sources and decide which content to cite when formulating answers.

    The first tactic centers on incorporating statistics, numbers, and verifiable proof throughout your content. AI models exhibit a strong preference for factual, data-backed information over general statements or opinions. When a model encounters two sources covering the same topic, one making vague claims and another providing specific numbers with citations, the statistical content almost always wins.

    This doesn't mean stuffing your content with random numbers. It means grounding your claims in specific, verifiable data wherever possible. Instead of writing "Our tool is widely used," you'd write "Our tool has 150,000 monthly active users with a 4.7 out of 5 satisfaction rating based on 3,200 reviews." The specificity signals credibility to AI models, which learned during training that precise data indicates reliable sources.

    The same principle applies to any factual claim. When discussing market trends, cite specific growth percentages and time periods. When mentioning firm performance, include actual revenue figures or user counts. When describing product features, provide concrete specifications rather than abstract descriptions. Each piece of specific data you add increases the likelihood that AI models will view your content as authoritative and citation-worthy.

    Sources indicate that this approach requires sourcing and maintaining accurate information, which means you can't fabricate numbers or exaggerate metrics. AI models increasingly cross-reference claims across sources, and inconsistencies damage credibility. The data you include must be truthful and, where relevant, attributed to primary sources. But when you consistently provide specific, accurate information, you build a reputation as a reliable source that AI models return to repeatedly.

    Industry observers note that the second tactic involves active engagement on Reddit, Quora, and similar community forums. This strategy works for a less obvious reason than you might expect. It's not primarily about direct traffic from forum posts, though that can be valuable. It's about creating authentic mentions and discussions of your content across platforms that AI models frequently encounter during training and web searches.

    Language models learn from vast datasets that include substantial amounts of community discussion content. Reddit threads, Quora answers, and forum posts represent genuine human conversations about real topics, making them high-value training data. When your content or expertise appears naturally in these discussions, it creates signals that AI models recognize and incorporate into their understanding of what resources exist and who's knowledgeable about specific topics.

    According to recent reports, the key word here is "naturally." AI models have learned to recognize and discount obvious spam, self-promotion, and link-dropping. Simply posting your URL in relevant threads won't help and might actually hurt if it generates negative reactions or gets flagged as spam. Instead, you need to participate genuinely in communities where your expertise is relevant, providing real value in discussions and mentioning your content only when it truly addresses someone's question or adds to the conversation.

    This means answering questions thoroughly, sharing insights from your experience, helping solve problems, and building a reputation as a knowledgeable contributor before you ever share links. When you do reference your content, it should be in the context of "I wrote a detailed guide about exactly this problem that covers X, Y, and Z" rather than "Check out my site." The former contributes to the discussion while the latter feels promotional.

    Recent findings suggest that over time, this authentic participation creates a distributed network of references to your expertise and content across platforms that AI models access. These organic mentions, especially when they're accompanied by positive community response, signal that you're a legitimate authority worth citing. The impact accumulates gradually but compounds over months as you build a presence in relevant communities.

    The third tactic focuses on optimizing for natural language queries rather than keyword stuffing. Traditional SEO often encourages optimizing for specific keyword phrases, sometimes at the expense of natural writing. You might structure sentences awkwardly to include exact keyword matches or repeat phrases more often than sounds natural. This approach can work for search engines that match keywords mechanically.

    AI models process language differently. They understand semantic meaning and context, not just keyword matching. When people query AI tools, they ask complete questions in conversational language: "What's the best WordPress hosting for SaaS applications?" rather than "WordPress hosting SaaS." Your content needs to answer these natural questions directly and comprehensively to appear in AI responses.

    Recent findings suggest that this means structuring your content around questions your audience actually asks. Include FAQ sections that address common queries in full-sentence question format. Write subheadings as questions rather than just topics. Provide complete answers that someone could understand without additional context. Make your content readable and helpful to humans first, trusting that AI models will recognize and value that quality.

    It has been revealed that the practical implementation involves thinking about the conversation your audience wants to have rather than the keywords they might type. What are they trying to accomplish? What confuses them? What decisions are they facing? What objections or concerns do they have? When you address these elements in natural, conversational language, you simultaneously create content that people find valuable and that AI models recognize as comprehensive answers to common questions.

    Industry observers note that the fourth tactic requires creating comparison tables and structured data that AI models can easily parse and reference. Language models excel at processing structured information organized in clear, consistent formats. When they encounter well-formatted comparison tables, step-by-step lists, or data organized in predictable structures, they can extract and cite that information more reliably than when similar content appears in dense paragraphs.

    This doesn't mean every piece of content should become a table or list. It means that when you're presenting information that naturally fits structured formats—comparisons between options, sequential steps in a process, multiple examples of a concept, sets of tips or recommendations—you should use formatting that makes that structure explicit and easy to process.

    In a recent development, for example, if you're comparing different software tools, create an actual comparison table with columns for features, pricing, pros, and cons rather than describing each tool in paragraph form. If you're explaining a multi-step process, number the steps and use consistent formatting for each. If you're providing examples, use a predictable structure where each example follows the same pattern.

    In a recent development, the benefit extends beyond AI optimization. Structured content is easier for human readers to scan and comprehend too. People increasingly skim content rather than reading every word, and clear structure helps them extract key information swiftly. When you optimize for both AI processing and human scanning through better structure, you improve the experience for all visitors while increasing AI citation rates.

    It has been revealed that implementation requires evaluating your existing content and identifying opportunities to add structure without forcing it artificially. Look for places where you're listing multiple items in prose that would be clearer as bullet points. Find sections comparing options that would benefit from table format. Identify processes that could be broken into numbered steps. These changes often improve content quality while making it more AI-friendly.

    It has been revealed that the fifth tactic involves building multi-platform authority by publishing consistent information across different channels. AI models, particularly those with web search capabilities, often cross-reference information across sources to verify accuracy and assess credibility. When they find the same core information presented consistently on your website, in your social media content, in articles you've published elsewhere, and in your responses on community platforms, it signals that you're a legitimate authority on that topic.

    In a recent development, this doesn't mean duplicating content identically across platforms, which could create SEO problems and doesn't align with best practices for different mediums. It means maintaining consistent expertise, perspectives, and factual information while adapting the format and style to each platform's norms and audience expectations.

    It has been revealed that your core message and expertise should be recognizable across a blog post on your website, a LinkedIn article, a Twitter thread, a YouTube video description, and a guest post on another site. The specific examples might vary, and the depth of coverage will differ based on format constraints, but the fundamental information should align. This consistency reinforces your authority and makes it easier for AI models to identify you as a reliable source on specific topics.

    Building this multi-platform presence takes time and consistent effort. You can't create authority across channels overnight, but you can develop a systematic approach to repurposing and adapting your best content for different platforms. Each piece of substantial content you create should have a distribution plan that gets the core insights in front of audiences across multiple channels over time.

    The strategic value compounds as your presence grows. Early on, you might only appear in AI responses when the model happens to encounter your website. As you build presence across platforms, the model has multiple opportunities to encounter your expertise from different angles, increasing the likelihood that it recognizes you as an authority worth citing.

    The sixth tactic emphasizes showing fresh revision signals throughout your content. AI models, especially those with real-time web access, demonstrate preference for current information over dated content. When choosing between two sources covering the same topic, with one clearly recent and another older, the fresher content usually gets cited unless there's a compelling reason to reference historical information.

    This creates both an opportunity and a maintenance requirement. The opportunity is that regularly updating content can improve AI citation rates even if the core information hasn't changed dramatically. The requirement is that high-performing content needs periodic refreshes to maintain its competitive position as newer articles on the same topics emerge.

    Making freshness obvious requires explicit signals that AI models can easily detect. The most straightforward approach is including "Last updated: [Date]" at the top of articles, making it immediately clear that the content reflects current information. This simple addition can significantly impact whether AI models view your content as relevant for queries about current state or recent developments.

    Beyond enhancement dates, freshness signals include referencing recent events, citing current statistics and data, mentioning the current year in context where relevant, and updating examples to reflect current tools and practices. These signals reassure both AI models and human readers that the information hasn't become outdated even if the core topic is relatively stable.

    The practical challenge is balancing the benefit of updates against the time investment required. You can't refresh every piece of content constantly, so prioritize based on importance and competitive pressure. Content that generates significant traffic or ranks well in AI responses deserves regular attention to maintain those positions. Content about rapidly changing topics needs more frequent updates than evergreen material. Content facing newly introduced competition from recently published articles needs refreshing to remain competitive.

    Sources indicate that implementing a content refresh schedule helps manage this systematically. Rather than updating randomly when you remember, establish a process where high-value content gets reviewed quarterly or semi-annually. During these reviews, patch statistics, add recent examples, remove dated references, and add the new update date. This structured approach ensures your most important content remains fresh without requiring constant attention to every article.

    The seventh tactic involves implementing JSON-LD structured data markup on your web pages. This technical optimization helps AI models understand your content's structure and purpose by providing machine-readable information about what your page contains, what type of content it is, and how different elements relate to each other.

    Structured data uses a standardized format called Schema.org vocabulary implemented through JSON-LD script tags. These tags don't affect how your content appears to human visitors, but they provide clear signals to automated systems parsing your pages, including AI models determining whether your content answers specific queries.

    Recent findings suggest that common structured data types relevant for most content include Article (marking blog posts and articles), HowTo (for step-by-step guides), FAQ (for question-and-answer sections), Person (for author bios), Organization (for company information), and Product (for product pages). Implementing appropriate schema markup for your content type helps AI models categorize and understand your content more accurately.

    The technical implementation requires adding JSON-LD scripts to your page HTML, typically in the header section. Many content management systems, including WordPress, offer plugins that generate this markup automatically based on your content, eliminating the need for manual coding. For custom implementations, Schema.org provides documentation and examples for each data type.

    It has been revealed that while structured data implementation requires more technical knowledge than the other tactics, its value extends beyond AIO. Search engines like Google also use structured data to create enhanced search results like rich snippets, knowledge panels, and featured answers. This means the optimization work benefits both traditional SEO and AI visibility simultaneously.

    Sources indicate that the cumulative effect of implementing all seven tactics is substantial. Content that includes specific statistics, appears in community discussions, answers natural language questions directly, presents information in structured formats, exists consistently across platforms, shows clear freshness signals, and implements proper schema markup sends multiple reinforcing signals that AI models recognize and value.

    Understanding individual tactics is important, but sustainable success requires integrating AIO into your overall content strategy rather than treating it as a separate, occasional activity. This means developing systematic approaches that maintain and improve your AI visibility over time without requiring constant manual intervention.

    It has been revealed that the next consideration is information density and specificity.     Industry observers note that establish monitoring routines to track your AI visibility over time.     Sources indicate that document what works as you implement and test different approaches.     Industry News: What Happier People Tend To Believe About Others

    📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (640 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Org

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.
    • A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.
    • Trusting others is linked to greater happiness and life satisfaction, a review involving over 2.5 million people finds.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.

    A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.

    Trusting others is linked to greater happiness and life satisfaction, a review involving over 2.5 million people finds.

    Happier people also tend to become more trusting over time.

    The link between trust and happiness is slightly stronger in children, adolescents and older adults, possibly because supportive relationships are especially crucial at these ages.

    Trust may help meet the need to belong by making it easier to build relationships in which people feel supported and secure.

    The research combined almost 1,000 findings from studies involving people aged six to 84.

    The analysis examined how trust related to everyday emotions, including happiness and sadness, as well as people’s overall satisfaction with their lives.

    Greater trust was consistently associated with better wellbeing.

    The association was somewhat stronger among children and adolescents than among young and middle-aged adults, and stronger among older adults than young adults.

    Trust may matter more at ages when people are building close relationships or becoming more dependent on others.

    For younger people, learning whom to trust is part of building meaningful friendships and supportive social networks.

    In later life, people may prioritise a smaller circle of close relationships and depend more on others for support.

    The researchers distinguished between trust in familiar people, trust in people generally and trust in institutions.

    The first involves confidence in someone known personally, such as a partner, friend or relative.

    General trust involves expectations about people more broadly, including strangers, while institutional trust concerns organisations such as governments, banks and the police.

    All three were associated with better wellbeing, but trust in familiar people showed the strongest connection.

    Trust may support wellbeing partly because close relationships require a willingness to be vulnerable.

    Expecting someone to respond with care can make it easier to seek help, cooperate and maintain a supportive connection.

    These relationships may satisfy the basic psychological need to feel connected to others and cared for in return.

    Trust could also provide a broader sense of security and predictability, making the social world feel more dependable.

    This may help explain why trust was slightly more closely related to overall life satisfaction than to positive or negative emotions.

    Life satisfaction reflects a broader assessment of how life is going, whereas emotions can fluctuate with immediate experiences.

    The relationship also worked in the other direction, with greater wellbeing predicting more trust later.

    One proposed explanation is that emotions influence how people interpret the world around them.

    Feeling happy may encourage more positive perceptions of other people, while anxiety may draw attention towards threats and uncertainty.

    Trust and wellbeing could therefore reinforce each other, with supportive expectations helping people feel better and positive feelings making trust easier.

    The wider social environment mattered too, with a stronger connection between trust and wellbeing in countries where people were generally more trusting.

    A trusting outlook may be more beneficial when the people around us are dependable.

    Simply encouraging someone to trust more overlooks the behaviour of the people and institutions receiving that trust.

    Professor Catrin Finkenauer, study co-author, stated:.

    “But trust can’t be forced—it has to be earned.”.

    The findings therefore highlight the importance of honesty, reliability, transparency and fair treatment in relationships and institutions.

    “When we build trust, we also support mental health and stronger communities.”.

    The study was published in the journal Psychological Bulletin (Bi et al., 2025).

    Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • What if you could ask your AI assistant how any app works and get a real answer, backed by evidence, without ever seeing the source code?
